title: Laryngology Fellowship
prerequisites: Audience: licensed/graduate physicians who completed OHNS residency or senior OHNS residents studying under appropriate supervision; the course is not suitable as authorization to diagnose/treat.
Foundation: laryngeal anatomy/physiology, clinical history, basic otolaryngology, interpretation of clinical evidence and professional privacy/consent obligations.
Institution-specific prerequisites differ; the official MEE page states ABOHNS certification or eligibility; MGH states completed OHNS residency. Verify current criteria directly.
objectives: Explain voice, swallowing and airway anatomy/physiology.
Apply a voice-focused history and dysphonia red-flag framework.
Describe endoscopic/stroboscopic observations while separating findings from inference.
Organize differential reasoning for benign lesions, inflammation, paralysis, airway disease and laryngeal neoplasia.
Recognize where multidisciplinary evaluation, further diagnostics, evidence appraisal and urgent escalation are appropriate.
Discuss high-level management categories and limitations without claiming procedural competence.

units.title: Upper aerodigestive anatomy, voice/swallow/airway physiology
objectives: Relate laryngeal subsites, innervation, mucosal wave and airway-protective closure to voice, breathing and swallow symptoms.
Explain the myoelastic-aerodynamic voice model and source-filter concept.
topics: Larynx, esophagus, tracheobronchial airway; embryology; respiration, cough, phonation and swallow physiology.
boardDomains: No separate laryngology examination blueprint identified; mapped to American Laryngological Association curriculum domains: Upper aerodigestive anatomy, voice/swallow/airway physiology

mapping.name: MEE Laryngology Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes one year, one position, multidisciplinary voice care, voice laboratory, pediatric airway exposure, phonomicrosurgery/laser, laryngeal cancer, framework surgery, LEMG, botulinum toxin and airway reconstruction. It lists four clinic sessions, four OR sessions and 0.5–1 day for research; page does not define every schedule detail. MEE page states ABOHNS certification or eligibility prerequisite; verify directly because volatile.

mapping.name: MGH Clinical Fellowship in Laryngeal Surgery
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Distinct official post-residency clinical and research fellowship page describes one- or two-year training, voice/airway/swallow, laryngeal cancer, paralysis, benign lesions, intubation injury, trauma, professional voice, inflammatory/connective tissue disorders, and research. The page states completed OHNS residency; no inference that MEE and MGH are one combined programme.

topicGaps: The 36-hour target remains unmet: 11.931389 unique verified public recording hours counted, leaving 24.068611 hours. This is an actual media-coverage gap, not a generated or planned-hour estimate.

The added recordings strengthen anatomy/voice production and perception, inflammatory/systemic laryngeal disease, inducible laryngeal obstruction, and swallow-screening concepts. They do not close the major lecture gaps in advanced dysphagia diagnostics, laryngeal cancer and premalignant lesions, benign lesion pathology, stenosis/trauma/reconstruction, pediatric/congenital laryngology, professional and gender-affirming voice care, outcomes/evidence appraisal, or detailed treatment options.

Public ALA curriculum PDFs and training guidelines provide topic maps and reading material, not a verified full-length lecture series or an independently validated clinical protocol. Some ALA content is dated (curriculum page says updated July 2019); disease-specific recommendations require current primary evidence and clinician review.

No public recording can substitute for in-person supervised endoscopy, LEMG, FEES/VFSS interpretation, operative/procedural experience, case volume, or fellowship assessment. The residual gap is not feasibly converted into 24 hours of verified external videos from the sources located in this review; any original lecture production remains scripted/planned, must be sourced and clinically reviewed, and cannot be claimed as rendered hours.

boardNames: American Board of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (ABOHNS): primary specialty certification in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery; no separate laryngology certificate/examination identified in the ABMS-listed subspecialty roster.
medical.boardStatus: Laryngology is an OHNS subspecialty/fellowship area, not a separate ABMS-listed board specialty/subspecialty. ABOHNS board certification is in OHNS; its US-residency pathway requires completion of ACGME-accredited OHNS residency plus then-current board requirements. Completion of either fellowship, this independent course, or an ALA-listed programme does not confer board eligibility or certification. No separate laryngology board examination identified as of 2026-10-07.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This is independent self-study and cannot establish eligibility for ABOHNS certification or any training program. MEE’s official page itself states ABOHNS certification or eligibility as an entry prerequisite; MGH states completed OHNS residency. Verify current pathways directly with the programme and board.

officialProgrammes.name: MEE Laryngology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes one year, one position, multidisciplinary voice care, voice laboratory, pediatric airway exposure, phonomicrosurgery/laser, laryngeal cancer, framework surgery, LEMG, botulinum toxin and airway reconstruction. It lists four clinic sessions, four OR sessions and 0.5–1 day for research; page does not define every schedule detail. MEE page states ABOHNS certification or eligibility prerequisite; verify directly because volatile.

officialProgrammes.name: MGH Clinical Fellowship in Laryngeal Surgery
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Distinct official post-residency clinical and research fellowship page describes one- or two-year training, voice/airway/swallow, laryngeal cancer, paralysis, benign lesions, intubation injury, trauma, professional voice, inflammatory/connective tissue disorders, and research. The page states completed OHNS residency; no inference that MEE and MGH are one combined programme.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet-listed official Mass General Brigham institutional pages verified 2026-10-07. Treat MEE one-year clinical offering and MGH one-/two-year clinical and research offering as exact separate variants; no combined programme stated. These are physician post-residency fellowships, not merely a directory category or non-physician research position. MGH separately describes a dedicated research fellowship option; it is not represented here as clinical-training equivalence. Public pages do not establish ACGME accreditation for these named programmes. ACGME’s current OHNS page lists OHNS and distinct Neurotology/Pediatric OHNS documents but no laryngology-specific requirement; ALA explicitly disclaims endorsement/accreditation of listed fellowships. ACGME listing alone is not proof of a program’s accreditation status.

Public ALA curriculum PDFs and training guidelines provide topic maps and reading material, not a verified full-length lecture series or an independently validated clinical protocol. practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with new dysphonia after recent chest surgery is otherwise stable. Which next principle best matches the 2018 AAO-HNSF dysphonia guideline?

options.text: Start empiric reflux medication based only on symptoms
Identify the recent surgery as a factor for expedited laryngeal evaluation
Order CT before visualizing the larynx in every case
Observe for six months before examining the larynx

practiceQuestions.rationale: Recent surgery involving head, neck or chest is a factor for expedited evaluation. The guideline recommends laryngoscopy when dysphonia has not improved within four weeks, or sooner if serious cause is suspected; it discourages CT/MRI before visualization for a primary voice complaint. This fictional question is educational, not a care directive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has persistent dysphonia for five weeks and is referred for voice therapy. What does the guideline recommend before voice therapy?

options.text: Diagnostic laryngoscopy and communication of results to the SLP
Routine CT regardless of visualization
Empiric antibiotics
Voice therapy without laryngeal examination

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline recommends diagnostic laryngoscopy before prescribing voice therapy and communication of results to the speech-language pathologist.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which claim about laryngology fellowship guidelines is supported by the ALA document?

options.text: ALA accredits every fellowship listed on its site
ALA guidelines identify laryngology as an OHNS subspecialty and are educational guidance, not accreditation
Laryngology fellowship completion grants ABOHNS certification
Every programme must have identical curriculum and case volumes

practiceQuestions.rationale: ALA describes laryngology as a subspecialty within OHNS and expressly says it takes no responsibility for endorsing listed fellowships; it does not claim accreditation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the correct board-certification distinction for this course?

options.text: It awards laryngology board certification
It substitutes for an ACGME OHNS residency
ABOHNS certifies OHNS; no separate laryngology board certificate/exam is listed by ABMS
ALA issues a laryngology board exam

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABMS lists ABOHNS OHNS certification and subspecialty certificates such as complex pediatric OHNS, neurotology, plastic surgery within head and neck, and sleep medicine; laryngology is not listed as a separate board certificate. This education course grants no credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient suddenly loses their singing voice after strenuous vocal use. What dangerous lesion belongs in the differential and needs prompt specialist assessment?

options.text: Vocal fold hemorrhage
Presbylaryngis by default
Reflux laryngitis as certain diagnosis
Nodule proven by symptom alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIDCD describes sudden hoarseness/voice loss after strenuous use as possible vocal fold hemorrhage requiring immediate voice rest and medical evaluation. Symptom alone does not establish the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about vocal fold paralysis is most accurate?

options.text: Unilateral paralysis always threatens ventilation more than bilateral disease
It can affect voice, breathing and swallowing; bilateral paralysis can be life-threatening
It has one known cause in every patient
It is diagnosed by voice quality alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIDCD notes paralysis may cause voice, breathing and swallowing symptoms; bilateral disease is rare and may be life-threatening. Causes may remain unknown; direct visualization is part of evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient presents with a primary voice complaint and no laryngeal visualization yet. Which imaging sequence aligns with the guideline?

options.text: Obtain CT/MRI before visualization in every patient
Do not obtain CT/MRI before laryngeal visualization solely for a primary voice complaint
Imaging replaces laryngoscopy
Imaging confirms histology

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline recommends against CT/MRI before laryngeal visualization for a primary voice complaint. Imaging decisions thereafter depend on the clinical findings and judgment.

title: Rhinology Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced physician learner: prior medical degree and completed or near-completed supervised otolaryngology–head and neck surgery residency-level foundations are assumed for the clinical reasoning; this is a course-level prerequisite, not an official MEE selection rule.
Comfort with sinonasal anatomy, basic pathology, clinical history/examination concepts, endoscopy and cross-sectional CT/MRI interpretation is expected.

The MEE public page does not state applicant eligibility criteria beyond post-residency advanced training; consult the programme directly. No fellowship admission or ABOHNS eligibility is conferred here.
Do not use this course to assess an actual patient, perform a nasal examination or procedure, order tests, select medicines, interpret images as a clinical report, or make a treatment decision.
objectives: Reason through common and complex rhinologic symptoms using appropriately dated evidence and explicit uncertainty.
Distinguish acute rhinosinusitis, CRS, rhinitis, CRSwNP, secondary CRS, complications, neoplasia and selected CSF-leak presentations using structured data gathering and differential diagnosis.
Explain CT/MRI roles, nasal/skull-base/orbital anatomy, medical and surgical management concepts, evidence outcomes, and key limitations without claiming procedural competence.
Map self-study to the broad public ABOHNS primary-certification domains relevant to nose/sinus care, while recognizing there is no separate published rhinology board blueprint or rhinology exam.
Recognize urgent features and the boundary where a qualified clinical team and local pathways are required.
Use authentic educational case links under their site-specific rights; never copy clinical images/patient records without permission.

assignment.title: Fictional rhinology evidence portfolio
assignment.instructions: Complete six fictional educational cases: (1) uncomplicated acute symptoms versus red flags; (2) symptoms with objective CRS data; (3) CRSwNP with asthma/AERD modifiers; (4) chronic unilateral symptoms with alternate diagnosis; (5) suspected CSF leak with imaging/lab evidence; (6) sinonasal mass imaging differential. For each: document observed evidence separately from inference; list at least two reasonable alternatives where appropriate; cite the current guideline/source; state what information is missing; identify urgent warning signs and escalation boundary; and include an image-rights note. These are not actual patients or patient records. Do not use copied proprietary cases/questions, download protected patient images, provide patient-specific advice, or produce a procedural plan.
deliverables: Six 300–500-word structured reasoning notes with references
One one-page update and source/provenance log
One rights attestation for each external case source
A 5–8-minute recorded verbal summary of one fictional case (no clinical image reuse)
assignment.gradingPlan: Formative rubric: 25% correct problem representation and differential; 25% objective evidence/data interpretation; 20% evidence recency/quality and citation; 20% uncertainty/red flags/supervision boundaries; 10% source and image-rights compliance. Any invented fact, copying of restricted content, or unsafe patient-specific advice requires correction before grading; no clinical sign-off.

assessment.format: Twelve unit checks, six fictional portfolio cases, one 10-item original formative practice set, plus guided source verification. Questions are new educational questions and not official or recalled board items.
assessment.passingClaim: No score predicts ABOHNS performance, establishes board eligibility, grants certification, or demonstrates clinical/procedural competence.
assessment.integrity: No proprietary ABOHNS exam questions or real patient records are used. Case scenarios written for the course are explicitly fictional; external authentic images remain linked at their lawful source.

unitMap.text: Sinonasal anatomy, physiology, histology and clinical safety frame
coveredTopics: Nasal cavity and sinus compartments; ostiomeatal complex; frontal recess and skull-base/orbital neighbors; mucociliary function; smell; histology; evidence and image provenance.

unitMap.text: Rhinitis, acute rhinosinusitis, epistaxis and urgent red flags
coveredTopics: Acute viral vs bacterial course; double-worsening/persistence; acute care; allergic/nonallergic rhinitis; epistaxis/HHT; orbital, intracranial and systemic warning features.

unitMap.text: CRS diagnosis, objective evidence, phenotype and outcomes
coveredTopics: CRS definitions; CRSsNP vs CRSwNP; clinical and objective criteria; nasal endoscopy; CT indications and limitations; differential diagnosis; SNOT-22 and quality-of-life concepts.

unitMap.text: Allergic/nonallergic rhinitis and topical medical therapy
coveredTopics: Allergy history/testing; vasomotor rhinitis; rhinitis medicamentosa differential; topical delivery and efficacy; intranasal therapy; immunotherapy principles; counseling and shared decisions.

unitMap.text: CRSwNP, type-2 inflammation, AERD and biologic decision concepts
coveredTopics: CRSwNP; phenotype/endotype language; AERD/NSAID-ERD; asthma; disease burden; biologic evidence and regulatory label verification; multidisciplinary discussion.

unitMap.text: Secondary/infectious CRS: CF, fungal disease, immune/ciliary conditions
coveredTopics: CF-related CRS; allergic fungal rhinosinusitis; acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis; systemic inflammatory/vasculitic disorders; immune evaluation; interdisciplinary care; differential and urgency.

unitMap.text: Nasal obstruction, septum/turbinate, pediatric and functional rhinoplasty
coveredTopics: Septal deviation; turbinate disorders; pediatric nasal obstruction; functional nasal valve/rhinoplasty concepts; smell and airflow; assessment and shared goals.

unitMap.text: Endoscopic sinus surgery indications, techniques, evidence and revision
coveredTopics: ESS history/indications; safe landmarks; balloon sinuplasty limits; outcomes; revision/extended maxillary and sphenoid surgery; postoperative care concepts; anatomy variation.

unitMap.text: Frontal sinus anatomy and advanced frontal surgery concepts
coveredTopics: Frontal recess; frontal sinus classifications at high level; disease patterns; extended approaches; risk structures; outcomes and follow-up.

unitMap.text: Anterior skull base, CSF rhinorrhea, encephalocele and reconstruction
coveredTopics: Traumatic/iatrogenic/spontaneous leak context; fluid confirmation; endoscopy; CT/MRI localization; encephalocele; reconstruction principles; recurrent/persistent leak; referral.

unitMap.text: Sinonasal tumors, orbital extension and lacrimal approaches
coveredTopics: Benign/fibro-osseous lesions; inverted papilloma and other tumors; sinonasal malignancy differential; anterior cranial fossa/orbit; endoscopic DCR; biopsy/planning concepts.

unitMap.text: Complications, outcomes, quality, integrated reasoning and exam-oriented synthesis
coveredTopics: Orbital/intracranial/vascular/CSF concerns; complication prevention; case review; quality and patient outcomes; evidence appraisal; primary certification domains; self-assessment.

topicGaps: Primary ABOHNS core ENT domains outside this rhinology-focused set, since rhinology-specific blueprint weighting is not public.
More updated, specialist-level CRSwNP/biologic evidence interpretation and patient preference; current AAO-HNS guidance is newer than several open lecture recordings.
Board-oriented integration of CRS phenotype, CT/endoscopy, comorbidity, outcomes and surgical decision reasoning.
Advanced endoscopic skull-base/CSF-leak differential and current lab/local pathway verification.
Image-based tumor/orbit and revision/frontal-sinus decision exercises that do not reuse protected patient images.
No validated score-to-board-performance relationship, hands-on operative training, procedural assessment or fellowship case experience.
The free public evidence found adds 4 verified items, but the observed unique recording total remains below the 36-hour floor; the remaining measured video deficit is not filled by planned scripts.
The 2024 public imaging lecture and the January 2025 biologics lecture are useful topic supplements, but neither replaces updated guideline review or local current imaging/drug-label verification.
The NIH grand-rounds hour includes broader head-and-neck anti-tumor immunity; only part of the session directly addresses olfactory neuroblastoma, so it is a partial rhinology fit.
The broad ABOHNS primary examination spans otolaryngology beyond rhinology; several parent-specialty domains remain outside this specialty-focused set and no rhinology exam/blueprint is published.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardStatus.primaryBoard: American Board of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (ABOHNS), primary certification in Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery.
boardStatus.status: ABOHNS is the relevant US primary specialty certifying board for the prerequisite specialty surrounding rhinology. ABOHNS lists nose/sinus diseases in primary otolaryngology scope and, as checked 2026-10-07, identifies its subspecialty subcertifications as Complex Pediatric Otolaryngology, Neurotology and Sleep Medicine. It does not list a rhinology subcertification or separate rhinology board examination. The American Rhinologic Society is a professional society, not a board certifier.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: No publicly published stand-alone rhinology exam blueprint or domain weightings were found. The curriculum is mapped pedagogically to publicly described ABOHNS primary assessment areas—basic science/physiology/pathophysiology, patient care, data gathering and interpretation, diagnosis, non-surgical management and surgical management—and to the board’s broad nose/sinus scope. This is not an official ABOHNS blueprint, endorsement, question bank, eligibility determination or exam predictor.
boardStatus.fellowshipAccreditation: The MEE and Harvard fellowship pages establish an institutional clinical fellowship and its broad goals, but do not state that this specific rhinology fellowship is ACGME-accredited. ACGME’s current OTO-HNS materials list Neurotology and Pediatric Otolaryngology subspecialty standards, not a rhinology accreditation standard. Accreditation status of the MEE fellowship is therefore not asserted.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course cannot establish ABOHNS eligibility, MEE fellowship eligibility, ACGME completion/accreditation, a qualifying prior residency, medical licensure, supervised experience/case volume, clinical or procedural competence, or certification. Rhinology has no separate ABOHNS subcertification/board exam listed as of 2026-10-07. Consult MEE, ACGME and ABOHNS directly for current programme/accreditation/eligibility facts.

officialProgrammes.name: MEE Rhinology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official MEE page states one year, two positions annually, advanced post-residency training of nasal, paranasal sinus and skull-base disease; minimally invasive sinonasal/orbital/skull-base approaches; and research opportunity. Fellows alternate every three months between two described services/faculty groups; time is balanced between OR and clinic, includes a weekly half-day ED preceptor role for PGY-2 residents and a protected weekly half-day for research/academic work. The page describes full-time duties. It does not publish a complete lecture sequence, case log, competency/case-volume thresholds, detailed rotations, ACGME accreditation claim, board examination, or individual eligibility criteria.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Official institutional pages establish that Mass Eye and Ear offers a one-year clinical Rhinology Fellowship within Harvard Otolaryngology. Its publicly described objectives and service pattern are summarized in the single exact institutional variant above. Public institutional programme information is not an ACGME determination, ABOHNS eligibility decision, full official curriculum, case log or proof of completion.
sourceCaveats: MEE is an official clinical fellowship listing in the Harvard-affiliated institutional directory. Its public description is not a complete fellowship curriculum, ACGME accreditation determination, case-volume report, or applicant eligibility rule.

No separate rhinology board examination/subcertification or publicly released rhinology-specific blueprint was found. The ABOHNS primary board scope is the proper high-level cognitive map; it cannot establish eligibility for a fellowship or primary board.
MEE fellowship page does not state accreditation status or exact applicant prerequisites. Do not infer ACGME accreditation from Harvard affiliation, the directory listing, or a clinical designation.
The 2025 AAO-HNSF update is the newest adult-sinusitis guideline located on the check date; 2020 EPOS and 2021 ICAR are context, not replacements for the newer guideline.

The 2016 CSF leak review and 2024 imaging review are learning sources, not current local protocols. Verify diagnostic laboratory methods, drug labeling, urgent pathways and treatment indications from current local/authoritative sources.

Video runtime is observed public metadata, not instructional efficacy or clinical credit. On 2026-10-07 the channel publicly listed 39 videos; 38 unique substantive IDs counted, intro/trailer excluded. Total counted duration is 79,100 seconds. No videos downloaded or rehosted.
Radiopaedia viewing is not blanket reuse permission. The ethmoidal meningocele case is explicitly excluded from licensing. The course stores only links, not images, case text, or patient records.

No human clinical review has been performed. This independent educational study does not confer Harvard/MEE/ABOHNS/ACGME affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, clinical or procedural competence, or certification; no passing guarantee.

topicGaps: Primary ABOHNS core ENT domains outside this rhinology-focused set, since rhinology-specific blueprint weighting is not public.
More updated, specialist-level CRSwNP/biologic evidence interpretation and patient preference; current AAO-HNS guidance is newer than several open lecture recordings.
Board-oriented integration of CRS phenotype, CT/endoscopy, comorbidity, outcomes and surgical decision reasoning.
Advanced endoscopic skull-base/CSF-leak differential and current lab/local pathway verification.
Image-based tumor/orbit and revision/frontal-sinus decision exercises that do not reuse protected patient images.
No validated score-to-board-performance relationship, hands-on operative training, procedural assessment or fellowship case experience.
The free public evidence found adds 4 verified items, but the observed unique recording total remains below the 36-hour floor; the remaining measured video deficit is not filled by planned scripts.
The 2024 public imaging lecture and the January 2025 biologics lecture are useful topic supplements, but neither replaces updated guideline review or local current imaging/drug-label verification.
The NIH grand-rounds hour includes broader head-and-neck anti-tumor immunity; only part of the session directly addresses olfactory neuroblastoma, so it is a partial rhinology fit.
The broad ABOHNS primary examination spans otolaryngology beyond rhinology; several parent-specialty domains remain outside this specialty-focused set and no rhinology exam/blueprint is published.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult has acute nasal obstruction and drainage for 4 days, is otherwise stable, and has no focal visual, neurological, or orbital findings. Which statement best reflects the current adult sinusitis guideline?

options.text: CT is required to distinguish viral from bacterial illness.
A 4-day course alone establishes acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and mandates antibiotics.
Uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis is commonly viral; routine imaging is not recommended unless complication or an alternative diagnosis is suspected.
CRS is established because symptoms are present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 AAO-HNSF update advises distinguishing presumed ABRS from viral/noninfectious disease and against imaging uncomplicated ARS absent concern for complications or another diagnosis. Duration alone at day 4 does not meet the guideline’s ABRS persistence or double-worsening criteria.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which evidence is needed to confirm a clinical diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis in an adult with prolonged symptoms?

options.text: Symptoms alone, regardless of duration.
Objective documentation of sinonasal inflammation by anterior rhinoscopy, nasal endoscopy, or CT.
A positive bacterial culture in every case.
A sinus CT before any clinical evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO-HNSF 2025 guideline recommends objective confirmation, which may be made through rhinoscopy, endoscopy, or CT; symptoms alone are insufficient.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with CRS but no nasal polyps asks whether a biologic should routinely be prescribed. Which answer aligns with the 2025 guideline?

options.text: Biologics should routinely be given to all CRS patients.
Biologics should not routinely be prescribed for CRS without polyps; the guideline distinguishes that group from CRSwNP discussions.
Biologics are indicated only after an allergy skin test.
The presence of any CT mucosal change is sufficient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KAS 13a recommends against routine biologics for adults with CRS without nasal polyps. In CRSwNP, patient education and individualized shared decision discussion are addressed separately.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional longitudinal history combines asthma, recurrent nasal polyps, and respiratory reactions after aspirin or another COX-1 inhibitor. Which course objective is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat this as unrelated symptoms and omit comorbidity review.
Recognize a pattern compatible with AERD/NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease and map it to specialist assessment and shared decision-making.
Assume aspirin challenge is safe to perform independently.
Conclude every such patient has fungal sinusitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AERD/NSAID-ERD is a relevant modifying phenotype/comorbidity in CRSwNP. Diagnosis, challenge/desensitization or treatment is not performed by self-study; use supervised specialty care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with unilateral clear rhinorrhea after craniofacial trauma raises concern for CSF leak. Which study approach best matches the reviewed principles?

options.text: Use a nasal glucose strip as a definitive test and skip imaging.
Treat the symptom alone as diagnostic.

Seek appropriate laboratory confirmation (commonly beta-2 transferrin where available) and specialist localization; thin-cut CT assesses bone, with MRI useful for soft tissue/meningoencephalocele questions.
Use CT cisternography on every suspected leak before any other assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open review emphasizes clinical, laboratory and imaging assessment; it regards glucose testing as unreliable, describes beta-2 transferrin as highly specific, and explains complementary CT/MRI roles. Local protocols and current lab methods govern.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected CRS has progressive proptosis, diplopia, reduced vision, or ophthalmoplegia. Which priority is safest?

options.text: Routine follow-up after saline trial.
Urgent in-person evaluation/escalation for possible orbital complication or alternate diagnosis.
Assume these features are typical of uncomplicated allergic rhinitis.
Wait for a public online case vote.

practiceQuestions.rationale: EPOS care pathways identify periorbital change, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia and reduced visual acuity as alarm symptoms requiring immediate referral. This is a red-flag learning item, not patient-specific triage advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner compares a sinonasal mass on CT and MRI. Which general imaging complement is most defensible?

options.text: CT is generally useful for bone and calcification; MRI offers soft-tissue contrast and helps assess perineural/dural extension; neither imaging pattern alone replaces diagnosis/staging.
MRI is always superior for bone erosion and CT cannot show anatomy.
A T2 signal alone proves a particular histology.
Imaging is unnecessary when a lesion is visible endoscopically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 open imaging review describes CT advantages for bone/anatomic features and MRI for soft tissue, perineural and dural extension; features are not uniquely diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an adult with uncomplicated CRS symptoms but no suspected acute complication, what objective methods can support inflammation confirmation according to the 2025 guideline?

options.text: Only culture.
Anterior rhinoscopy, nasal endoscopy, or CT.
Only plain sinus radiographs.
Routine MRI for every patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 guideline explicitly permits anterior rhinoscopy, endoscopy, or CT for objective documentation. Test choice remains clinical and context-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees an authentic case on Radiopaedia and wants to paste images into a course deck. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Copy because public viewing equals public domain.
Link learners to the source and check the exact case-level status and terms; reuse only if its license permits the intended use with attribution/share-alike/noncommercial conditions.
Remove attribution and crop out metadata.
Download screenshots since the case is de-identified.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia states CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 terms apply, but specifically excluded cases exist. Public access is not public domain; the ethmoidal meningocele case in this curriculum is excluded from licensing and must not be reused.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about this course’s board alignment is accurate?

options.text: Rhinology is an ABOHNS subcertification exam and completion here establishes eligibility.

ABOHNS lists a primary otolaryngology assessment and three subcertification fields; it does not list rhinology as a distinct subcertification. This independent course maps to broad primary domains but grants no eligibility.
Mass Eye and Ear’s fellowship page guarantees ABOHNS eligibility.
Course completion confers surgical competence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOHNS lists Complex Pediatric Otolaryngology, Neurotology, and Sleep Medicine subcertifications; the nose and sinus are included within primary otolaryngology scope. This source does not establish the ACGME status or eligibility of the specific MEE fellowship, and course study confers none.

topicGaps: Verified external recording time is 2.555 hours of the 36-hour target (1.577778 specialty and 0.977222 foundation hours); the actual residual is 33.445 hours. Authored scripts and all targetMinutes values are not rendered videos and add zero verified hours.

ASPO lists 30 specialty recordings, but public runtime/access was not verified for those individual Drive links; they remain duration-unknown and uncounted. The 2025 AAO-HNS Global Grand Rounds event has no established open replay and the event page states no external use or transfer.

The added Stanford recording gives one 94:40 case-based, multidisciplinary aerodigestive seminar. The two Mayo recordings are family-facing foundations and do not substitute for advanced diagnostic audiology, operative instruction, or supervised case conferences.

Insufficient verified long-form instruction remains for acute/chronic ear disease, complex airway and stenosis, tracheostomy longitudinal safety, sleep-disordered breathing, sinonasal emergencies, cleft/craniofacial care, vascular/head-and-neck masses, cholesteatoma, voice, oncology, and quality improvement; authored scripts address selected reasoning concepts only.

Open-airway examination, endoscopy, procedures, operative judgment, supervised clinical case volume, longitudinal outcomes, family consent, and emergency response cannot be acquired through this self-study curriculum.

medical.boardStatus: Pediatric otolaryngology is within primary ABOHNS certification scope. A separate CPO subcertification examination exists; passing alone does not confer subcertification. ABOHNS identifies CPO as one of its three subcertifications. ACGME-accredited fellowship completion and other board eligibility requirements apply; current 2026 exam sequencing/eligibility is time-sensitive and candidates must consult ABOHNS directly. This course offers no eligibility or certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABOHNS states primary certification requires accredited residency and passing written and oral examinations. MEE states its programme requires graduation from an ACGME-accredited otolaryngology–head and neck surgery residency. That institutional admission rule is not itself proof of any applicant's board eligibility. The separate CPO subcertification is for complex pediatric practice, not a universal credential needed to care for children. Verify current Training Pathway criteria, application windows, exam sequence, and timelines directly with ABOHNS.

unknownDurationItems.title: ASPO COVID-era Pediatric Otolaryngology Lecture and Video Series (30 linked lecture recordings; named item ledger in MED-X075-lecture-evidence.json)
unknownDurationItems.reason: Accessible duration not structurally supported by evidence.

topicGaps: Verified external recording time is 2.555 hours of the 36-hour target (1.577778 specialty and 0.977222 foundation hours); the actual residual is 33.445 hours. Authored scripts and all targetMinutes values are not rendered videos and add zero verified hours.

ASPO lists 30 specialty recordings, but public runtime/access was not verified for those individual Drive links; they remain duration-unknown and uncounted. The 2025 AAO-HNS Global Grand Rounds event has no established open replay and the event page states no external use or transfer.

The added Stanford recording gives one 94:40 case-based, multidisciplinary aerodigestive seminar. The two Mayo recordings are family-facing foundations and do not substitute for advanced diagnostic audiology, operative instruction, or supervised case conferences.

Insufficient verified long-form instruction remains for acute/chronic ear disease, complex airway and stenosis, tracheostomy longitudinal safety, sleep-disordered breathing, sinonasal emergencies, cleft/craniofacial care, vascular/head-and-neck masses, cholesteatoma, voice, oncology, and quality improvement; authored scripts address selected reasoning concepts only.

Open-airway examination, endoscopy, procedures, operative judgment, supervised clinical case volume, longitudinal outcomes, family consent, and emergency response cannot be acquired through this self-study curriculum.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 6-week-old infant does not pass a newborn hearing screen. What is the most appropriate interpretation of that screening result?

options.text: It establishes permanent bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
It warrants timely diagnostic evaluation, typically by pediatric audiology; it does not by itself establish type or severity.
It rules out hearing loss if the infant responds to voices.
It is an indication for immediate cochlear implantation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIDCD distinguishes screening from follow-up diagnostic assessment and recommends prompt pediatric audiology after a screen suggesting possible loss; treatment decisions require confirmation and individualized evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best captures the role of OAE and ABR in newborn hearing screening?

options.text: They are equivalent diagnostic measures of behavioral speech perception.
OAE assesses an ear acoustic response and ABR assesses auditory nerve/brainstem response; either screening result requires context and appropriate follow-up.
ABR identifies the genetic cause of hearing loss.
OAE directly measures the child's language development.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIDCD describes OAE and ABR mechanisms, but screening tests do not independently define etiology or communication function.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has bilateral middle-ear effusion documented for more than three months and caregiver concern about hearing. Which next educational response best aligns with current tube-guideline reasoning?

options.text: Ignore hearing because effusion is always asymptomatic.
Review hearing evaluation, developmental risk and the 2022 guideline's candidacy framework with the family and treating team.
Recommend tubes for every single episode of acute otitis media.
Treat the case as an emergency operation without further assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2022 AAO-HNSF guideline addresses children aged 6 months–12 years being considered for tubes and centers evidence-based patient selection; clinical decisions require hearing/development context and shared decision-making.

practiceQuestions.stem: A family reports a child's snoring and daytime symptoms. What is the most defensible guideline-based teaching point before an elective tonsillectomy discussion?

options.text: Symptoms alone always prove obstructive sleep apnea.
Use age- and risk-aware evaluation; the AAO-HNSF guideline addresses polysomnography and recommends tonsillectomy for OSA documented by overnight PSG, with shared discussion of context and risks.
Polysomnography has no role in pediatric decision-making.
All snoring requires immediate surgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO-HNSF 2019 guideline applies to children 1–18 years and includes PSG-related key actions. This item avoids turning a guideline into an automatic indication.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has nasal discharge and daytime cough for 11 days without improvement after a URI. According to the cited 2013 AAP sinusitis guideline, which pattern is described?

options.text: Persistent illness pattern; this is an older dated guideline and current updates should be checked.
Severe onset by definition.
A bacterial diagnosis is excluded because discharge is not purulent.
A sinus CT is mandatory for all such children.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAP guideline describes persistent symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement, alongside worsening and severe-onset patterns. It dates to 2013 and should not be treated as proof of current recommendations without an update check.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn has intermittent stridor and feeding difficulty. Which first reasoning step is safest in a case conference?

options.text: Assume benign laryngomalacia and defer assessment.
Assess stability and red flags, characterize timing/quality and feeding/voice associations, then plan supervised age-appropriate evaluation and escalation.
Recommend an unsupervised airway procedure.
Use adult airway anatomy as an equivalent substitute.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requirements emphasize assessment of neonates through adolescents with airway and other pediatric disorders, patient safety and appropriate care. Symptoms alone do not establish diagnosis; this course does not teach independent procedures.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ACGME pediatric otolaryngology requirements is correct?

options.text: They certify any online learner after 12 months of study.
They define standards for accredited graduate medical education programmes, including a 12-month educational programme; they do not make this independent course accredited training.
They guarantee fellowship admission to a learner who completes all units.
They are an ABOHNS board examination blueprint.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 ACGME source is programme requirements; a minimum educational programme length is not equivalent to independent coursework, licensure, or board certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which credential statement is accurate as of the board sources checked on 2026-10-07?

options.text: Every pediatric otolaryngologist must pass a separate CPO exam to be covered by primary certification.
Pediatric otolaryngology is included in primary ABOHNS certification scope; CPO is a separate subcertification with additional requirements and exam.
The CPO exam alone awards subcertification.
There is no CPO subcertification exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOHNS says pediatric otolaryngology is comprehensively covered by initial certification and describes CPO subcertification for especially complex pediatric cases. Passing an exam alone is not subcertification.

practiceQuestions.stem: An instructor wants to use an ASPO-linked operative clip inside a new course. What is the appropriate rights practice?

options.text: Public viewing automatically permits downloading and rehosting.
Link to the original host, check its current access and rights/privacy conditions, and do not copy/rehost patient media without authorization.
Remove the channel logo and reuse freely.
Assume every clinical image is de-identified.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ASPO page links externally hosted media, which does not itself convey reuse permission or certify patient de-identification. This course links rather than reproduces it.

practiceQuestions.stem: What can a learner infer from the MEE fellowship page's statement that its one-year programme has been ACGME accredited since 2005?

options.text: All learners in this online course can claim ACGME training.
MEE reports its fellowship programme accreditation history; it says nothing by itself about an individual learner's eligibility, skills, licensure or board status.
The course guarantees a fellowship position.
ACGME accredits the ABOHNS exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Institutional programme facts and learner credentials are different evidence categories. MEE's published description does not confer any status on a self-study learner.

topicGaps: The 2025 ABOS Shoulder/Elbow continuing-certification blueprint includes trauma, reconstruction, instability, neurovascular, and general domains. This self-study course is not an official exam simulation or eligibility pathway.

Unit 6 has one newly verified short proximal-humerus OTA lecture and public AO reference; no long-form video was verified for all shoulder-girdle fracture topics (clavicle, scapula, humeral shaft, malunion/nonunion).

Elbow fracture evaluation/fixation is represented by existing broad ASES difficult-case lectures and AO linked reference, but no distinct, full-length verified lecture for each distal-humerus, olecranon, radial-head, and coronoid topic was added.

Unit 12 research design, bias/confounding, and oral-case synthesis remain mostly course-authored assignments; the new ASES/ORS webinar is shoulder research content, not a comprehensive methods course.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A guideline’s stated population is adults with rotator cuff injuries. Which use best respects its scope when considering an adolescent patient?

options.text: Apply every recommendation unchanged because tendon anatomy is shared.
Recognize the guideline excludes pediatric patients and seek age-appropriate evidence and specialist judgment.
Assume the guideline proves surgery is contraindicated.
Use the guideline only if MRI confirms a full-thickness tear.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 AAOS guideline expressly addresses adult patients and is not intended for pediatric rotator cuff injuries; a scope boundary is not a treatment recommendation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reads the AAOS glenohumeral OA guideline and applies it to post-infectious arthropathy. What is the principal limitation?

options.text: The guideline scope is primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis and excludes post-infectious and other etiologies.
The guideline addresses elbow, not shoulder.
It applies only to pediatric patients.
The guideline addresses diagnosis but never management.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official page lists multiple excluded etiologies, including post-infectious arthropathy; do not generalize its recommendations outside scope.

practiceQuestions.stem: As of the board pages checked 7 October 2026, which statement most accurately characterizes shoulder/elbow board credentials?

options.text: ABOS awards an initial Shoulder/Elbow subspecialty certificate after any one-year fellowship.
ASES match completion is a board examination.
ABOS lists Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine subspecialty certificates; it separately lists a practice-profiled Shoulder/Elbow continuing-certification exam.
No ABOS examination ever addresses shoulder/elbow practice.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS states it offers two subspecialty certificates, Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine; its continuing certification page separately lists a Shoulder/Elbow practice-profiled exam. These are distinct from fellowship completion.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional adult with recurrent anterior shoulder instability after multiple episodes. Which response is the best next reasoning step before selecting a procedure?

options.text: Assume soft-tissue stabilization is always sufficient.
Assess history, examination, associated injury and glenoid/humeral bone-loss questions; select imaging to answer the planning question.
Diagnose posterior instability from recurrence alone.
Skip neurovascular assessment if the shoulder is reduced.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reasoning should integrate recurrence, examination, associated injury and bone-loss assessment; a vignette alone does not establish a procedure or a diagnostic certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has pain after reverse shoulder arthroplasty. Which approach is most defensible at the start of evaluation?

options.text: Assume baseplate loosening and proceed directly to revision.
Construct a differential that includes infection, instability, fracture, fixation, nerve and non-implant causes; then direct evaluation to findings.
Attribute pain to normal aging without examination.
Use a single normal radiograph to exclude all complications.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Painful arthroplasty evaluation is differential-driven. Public ASES educational content addresses painful reverse TSA, but cannot replace clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case includes elbow dislocation plus possible fracture and hand paresthesia. What should the learner prioritize in the case presentation?

options.text: Document neurovascular status and identify associated fracture/stability questions before treating it as a simple dislocation.
Omit nerve examination because paresthesia is expected.
Assume the fracture is a radial-head fracture without imaging.
Discuss only long-term rehabilitation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The combination raises associated-injury and neurovascular concerns; the case needs a complete assessment and imaging rationale rather than unsupported assumptions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public surgical teaching video is freely viewable. What may a curriculum builder safely infer?

options.text: Free viewing automatically grants permission to download and republish every patient image.
It can be linked for study subject to access terms; public viewing alone does not grant copying/republication rights.
Any image in it is guaranteed de-identified.
The video substitutes for supervised procedural competence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free access and reuse licensing are separate. This course links videos and does not copy case images or claim procedural credentialing.

practiceQuestions.stem: The public MGB fellowship page describes faculty-led research and clinical consultation sessions but provides no numeric case-volume promise. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: A learner may claim an exact minimum operative volume from this page.
The public page describes those educational elements; it does not establish a numeric volume or complete private didactic curriculum.
The course reproduces the institutional fellowship.
The institution’s page proves ACGME accreditation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official public description supports the published elements but does not provide every curriculum detail, case count or accreditation claim.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 2025 AAOS rotator cuff recommendation seems relevant to an adult vignette. What is the best method of use?

options.text: Treat it as an inflexible order for every patient.
Read the recommendation strength and evidence scope, then integrate individual findings, goals, alternatives and uncertainty.
Assume any patient who differs from the guideline received substandard care.
Ignore the guideline’s evidence review and follow a video technique.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical practice guidelines synthesize evidence but do not eliminate individualized decision-making; AAOS provides the full guideline and review report.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow cites an outcome series associating a technique with improved function. Which appraisal question is most useful before claiming causation?

options.text: Could selection, confounding, follow-up, outcome measurement, or loss to follow-up explain some of the association?
Was the title memorable?
Did the series use a shoulder implant?
Can the association be converted directly into an individual prediction?

practiceQuestions.rationale: Study design, confounding, follow-up, and outcome validity constrain causal inference and generalization; a series cannot alone predict an individual result.

assignment.title: Fictional case conference and evidence audit

assessment.format: 12 original formative MCQs, unit memos and fictional capstone case presentation.

boardNames: American Board of Orthopaedic Surgery (ABOS): primary general orthopaedic certification; Adult Reconstruction practice-profiled Continuing Certification examination (not separate ABOS adult-reconstruction subspecialty certificate)
medical.boardStatus: ABOS lists Hand Surgery and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine as its two subspecialty certificates. Adult reconstruction appears as a practice-profiled Continuing Certification examination for ABOS Diplomates, not an initial fellowship subspecialty exam.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: No eligibility or credential is conferred. MGH public applicant criteria state US residency graduate and board eligible; BWH page reviewed does not specify entry criteria. ACGME requirements describe an accredited 12-month fellowship but do not establish accreditation of these specific programs. Verify institutional and ABOS requirements directly.

officialProgrammes.name: MGH Adult Reconstructive Surgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official description: 12-month clinical work; five 10-week rotations with seven surgeons; daily 6:45 conference, weekly indications conference, lectures/journal club, cadaver labs; hip/knee primary/revision experience; two research projects. MGH says applicants must be graduates of US residency programs and board eligible. Public summary is not a full syllabus.

officialProgrammes.name: BWH Total Joint Arthroplasty Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official description: total joint arthroplasty, primary/revision patient care, teaching and research; program says over 350 cases as surgeon or first assistant (not an independently audited guarantee). SF Match is stated. Prerequisites/full syllabus not disclosed on reviewed page.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Two separate institutional clinical-physician fellowships, not a combined program or generic category. Not a research-only/non-physician supplement. ACGME has subspecialty requirements, but no specific-site accreditation confirmation is claimed.
sourceCaveats: Guidelines and board status checked 2026-10-07; verify updates before use.

practiceQuestions.stem: Painful THA with elevated ESR and CRP: best interpretation?

options.text: PJI is proven.
PJI is excluded.
Use as diagnostic adjuncts in a broader, timing-sensitive evaluation.
Peripheral leukocyte count is more reliable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAOS supports ESR/CRP as useful adjuncts, not stand-alone diagnoses.

practiceQuestions.stem: Stable fictional patient suspected of PJI with cultures planned: which principle?

options.text: Always start antibiotics first.
When clinically safe, obtain cultures before antimicrobial initiation; do not delay urgent sepsis care.
Avoid cultures.
Use only peripheral WBC.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAOS supports avoiding antimicrobials until cultures/diagnosis in stable suspected cases; sepsis is not delayed.

practiceQuestions.stem: In recurrent THA instability, what concept supplements static component position?

options.text: Functional spinopelvic mechanics and patient history.
Ignore lumbar history.
One universal target fits all.
Dual mobility eliminates all risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAHKS FOCAL catalog addresses hip-spine, spinopelvic mechanics and instability; options remain individualized.

practiceQuestions.stem: Best interpretation of robotic/navigation lecture claims?

options.text: Robot proves superior outcomes in all cases.
Technical alignment accuracy is not automatically improved patient-important outcome.
Technology replaces patient selection.
All systems equivalent.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Critically distinguish process measures and clinical outcomes.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional UKA decision: sound framework?

options.text: Assess compartment disease, symptoms, anatomy, alignment and patient factors; compare options.
Select by one x-ray feature.
UKA/TKA indications identical.
Ignore symptoms.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Case-based AAHKS content and AAOS knee OA guidance support deliberate individualized choice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional painful, stiff TKA: first stance?

options.text: Label arthrofibrosis without evaluation.
Consider infection, mechanical and extra-articular causes; gather history/exam/records.
All pain is loosening.
Revise from vignette alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A differential-first approach matches painful TKA/stiffness education and preserves uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: Revision THA lacks op report and implant identification. Next step?

options.text: Proceed from webinar image.
Retrieve history/implant information and characterize failure before planning.
Assume same extraction for all implants.
Copy source video.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Source revision content highlights implant identification; no webinar substitutes for patient records/supervised judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Periprosthetic fracture: missing implant stability/bone stock. Best answer?

options.text: Classify from age alone.
Name missing imaging, fracture pattern, implant stability, bone stock and patient context.
Choose fixation without data.
Always revise.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fracture pathway is context dependent; broad-source case conference does not establish simplified rule.

practiceQuestions.stem: ABOS adult reconstruction status?

options.text: Separate certificate just like hand.
Hand/sports are ABOS subspecialty certificates; adult reconstruction is practice-profiled continuing certification, not a separate initial certificate.
This course grants eligibility.
Blueprint is fellowship entrance exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS sources make distinction explicit.

practiceQuestions.stem: 2025 ABOS adult reconstruction blueprint targets?

options.text: Hip 40%, knee 40%, perioperative 10%, general 10%.
Hip 50%, knee 50%.
Hip 10%, knee 10%, perioperative 80%.
Equal.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Published targeted proportions; an individual examination may vary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional pre-op patient has infection/recovery risk factors. What fits this course?

options.text: Automatically clear.
Flag factors for clinical team review; do not issue patient clearance.
Guarantee optimization removes risk.
Assume all factors are absolute contraindications.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Risk evidence is graded/context dependent; self-study does not substitute for clinician assessment.

title: Head and Neck Radiology Fellowship
prerequisites: Completed diagnostic radiology residency is stated as the official MEE fellowship prerequisite; this independent self-study is aimed at radiology residents/fellows and qualified radiologists.
Working knowledge of cross-sectional anatomy, CT/MR/US physics and image interpretation.
Ability to access and interpret cases only under source repository rules; no patient records or credentialed viewer accounts supplied.
objectives: Interpret head and neck findings using a systematic compartmental and modality-aware approach.
Recognize published ABR neuroradiology H&N domains and distinguish them from an independent H&N board credential.
Use current ACR practice parameters and reporting systems critically; verify active revision and contextual exceptions.
Generate a clear observation-led differential and report with limitations, uncertainty and appropriate escalation.
Analyze authentic but linked case resources under their de-identification, controlled-access and reuse requirements.
Describe but do not independently perform or authorize image-guided procedures, clinical protocols or treatment.

assignment.title: Capstone: multimodality H&N case conference memo
assignment.instructions: For one authorized TCIA dataset example or a wholly fictional written case, prepare a 1–2 page problem representation, anatomic localization, modality/protocol reasoning, structured observable findings, differential, limitations, and one question for a hypothetical multidisciplinary team. Do not download or redistribute facially reconstructable data without approved access; no screenshots or patient records in submissions. Include citations and applicable dataset attribution.
assignment.scoring: 100-point formative rubric; this course sets no pass threshold, does not validate competency and is not a board-passing predictor.

assessment.format: Formative self-checks after each unit, 10 original MCQs, three short image-free case memos using authorized linked resources or fictional text, and capstone conference memo.
assessment.rubric: Rubric: correct regional localization 25%, defensible modality and exam limits 20%, observable evidence versus inference 20%, safety/privacy/rights 20%, citations and communication 15%. No credit substitutes for supervised case review.
assessment.masteryNotice: Not validated; not official ABR content; cannot predict or guarantee examination outcome.

unitMap.text: Clinical question, modality, protocol and image quality
coveredTopics: CT/MR/US role; contrast and spatial resolution; image quality/artifacts; dose and safety; structured report and communication.

unitMap.text: Skull base, cranial foramina, sella and perineural routes
coveredTopics: Anterior/middle/posterior skull base; foramina; sella; pterygopalatine fossa; cranial nerves; perineural tumor spread; artifacts and variants.

unitMap.text: Orbit, ophthalmic and visual pathway imaging
coveredTopics: Orbital bones and compartments; optic nerve/chiasm; extraocular muscles; inflammatory/infectious, vascular, neoplastic, traumatic/post-treatment patterns.

unitMap.text: Sinonasal cavity and facial bones
coveredTopics: Paranasal sinus anatomy; ostiomeatal drainage; Keros/olfactory fossa; Onodi and Haller variants; sinusitis; fungal/invasive infection; neoplasia; trauma and postoperative FESS.

unitMap.text: Temporal bone, otologic imaging and hearing loss
coveredTopics: High-resolution CT, MRI labyrinth/IAC; ossicles, facial nerve, labyrinth, petrous apex; cholesteatoma patterns; congenital anomalies; labyrinthitis; surgical change.

unitMap.text: CPA/IAC, cranial nerves and skull-base extension
coveredTopics: IAC, CPA, cranial nerve pathways, facial nerve, vascular variants, enhancing masses, inflammatory and perineural spread.

unitMap.text: Suprahyoid/infrahyoid spaces and cervical fascial anatomy
coveredTopics: Deep cervical fascia, carotid, visceral, prevertebral, parapharyngeal, masticator, parotid, submandibular, retropharyngeal and pharyngeal mucosal spaces.

unitMap.text: Neck masses, nodal stations, infection and vascular mimics
coveredTopics: Cervical nodal levels; inflammatory/infectious, congenital, salivary, neoplastic and vascular lesions; dental artifact; deep neck infection; airway/mediastinal extension.

unitMap.text: Thyroid and parathyroid: ultrasound, cross-sectional imaging and systems
coveredTopics: US anatomy; ACR TI-RADS; incidental nodule; parathyroid localization imaging; thyroid cancer staging; ectopic glands; limitations of 4D-CT and radiation.

unitMap.text: Pharynx, larynx, oral cavity and oncologic imaging
coveredTopics: Nasopharynx/oropharynx/hypopharynx/larynx/oral cavity; SCC; HPV/EBV context; salivary/perineural routes; imaging staging; response and reconstruction.

unitMap.text: Post-treatment disease, treatment effects and NI-RADS concept
coveredTopics: Treatment effects, altered anatomy, flap/reconstruction, PET/CT context, NI-RADS role, longitudinal comparison and communication.

unitMap.text: Pediatric, congenital, trauma, infection and safe communication synthesis
coveredTopics: Congenital temporal bone and neck lesions; pediatric orbit/sinus/neck; fracture and blunt injury; invasive infection; dose minimization; post-procedural states; ethics/privacy.

topicGaps: Dedicated parathyroid localization, ectopic glands and 4D-CT/US/MR trade-offs remain insufficiently covered by verified teaching.
Current, complete TI-RADS lexicon/scoring and contextual rules must be checked in active ACR source materials; the two added recordings date from 2018.
Detailed salivary-gland neoplasm differential, perineural routes and site-specific oncologic staging need more current, source-grounded instruction.
Formal current NI-RADS modality-specific MRI/CT/PET criteria and flowchart application remain a gap because ACR content is dynamically rendered; no category thresholds are inferred from older videos.

Pediatric congenital and cystic masses have one relevant case-review recording, but pediatric trauma, protocol/dose application, infection red flags and vascular anomalies remain insufficiently taught.

Additional systematic, case-based instruction is needed for orbit, skull-base/sella, CPA/IAC, facial trauma, vascular mimics, treatment effects and current tumor staging across the complete ABR H&N blueprint.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

topicGaps: Dedicated parathyroid localization, ectopic glands and 4D-CT/US/MR trade-offs remain insufficiently covered by verified teaching.
Current, complete TI-RADS lexicon/scoring and contextual rules must be checked in active ACR source materials; the two added recordings date from 2018.
Detailed salivary-gland neoplasm differential, perineural routes and site-specific oncologic staging need more current, source-grounded instruction.
Formal current NI-RADS modality-specific MRI/CT/PET criteria and flowchart application remain a gap because ACR content is dynamically rendered; no category thresholds are inferred from older videos.

Pediatric congenital and cystic masses have one relevant case-review recording, but pediatric trauma, protocol/dose application, infection red flags and vascular anomalies remain insufficiently taught.

Additional systematic, case-based instruction is needed for orbit, skull-base/sella, CPA/IAC, facial trauma, vascular mimics, treatment effects and current tumor staging across the complete ABR H&N blueprint.
