practiceQuestions.stem: In an imaging examination for bony ossicles and temporal-bone detail, which examination is generally the more direct anatomic choice?

options.text: Dedicated high-resolution CT
Routine chest radiograph
Carotid duplex alone
Noncontrast abdominal MRI

practiceQuestions.rationale: CT best resolves fine osseous structures; protocol choice remains dependent on question, patient and local standards. This is educational, not a patient-specific order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a unilateral visual field deficit described as bitemporal. Which adjacent compartment deserves careful review for a compressive lesion?

options.text: Optic chiasm/sellar-suprasellar region
External auditory canal
Submandibular space
Mastoid antrum

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bitemporal field loss localizes classically to crossing fibers at the optic chiasm; the course asks learners to target anatomy and confirm clinical details rather than assume cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which structure normally traverses the optic canal?

options.text: Optic nerve and ophthalmic artery
Facial nerve and internal jugular vein
Vagus nerve and carotid artery
Glossopharyngeal nerve and sigmoid sinus

practiceQuestions.rationale: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery; distinguish this from contents of the superior orbital fissure.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypothetical temporal-bone soft-tissue focus is described near the epitympanum. What is the best first reporting habit?

options.text: Describe exact location, ossicular/scutum relationship and bony change before a categorical diagnosis
Call it cholesteatoma solely because it is soft tissue
Omit comparison with prior studies
Infer pathology from the referral phrase alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Anatomic localization and observable features support the differential; a single sign is insufficient for a definitive label.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does ACR TI-RADS apply to?

options.text: Ultrasound-based thyroid nodule risk stratification/reporting
Post-treatment head and neck cancer surveillance
Prostate cancer MRI scoring
Liver lesion risk classification

practiceQuestions.rationale: TI-RADS is thyroid imaging, reporting and data system; do not transpose it to unrelated organs or conditions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most defensible way to use TI-RADS in a course exercise?

options.text: Verify the current lexicon, point system and recommendation thresholds from ACR source
Treat a category as histologic proof of malignancy
Ignore size and clinical context in all cases
Apply the label to any neck mass

practiceQuestions.rationale: TI-RADS is a reporting/management aid; current recommendations and clinical context matter. ACR FAQ lists important exceptions.

practiceQuestions.stem: NI-RADS is principally intended to standardize reporting for which context?

options.text: Imaging surveillance after treatment for head and neck cancer
Primary breast screening
Acute stroke thrombectomy selection
Prostate MRI biopsy targeting

practiceQuestions.rationale: NI-RADS is the ACR Neck Imaging Reporting and Data System; its specific current criteria should be checked in the current ACR source.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional neck lesion is centered in a specific fascial space. Why is this location useful?

options.text: It narrows a differential by structures and boundaries of that compartment
It proves the lesion is malignant
It removes the need for clinical history
It determines biopsy safety automatically

practiceQuestions.rationale: Compartmental anatomy helps localize origin and narrow the differential, but does not prove pathology or authorize an intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which list matches the published ABR neuroradiology Head & Neck exam regions?

options.text: Orbit; sinonasal/facial bones; skull base; CPA/IAC; temporal bone; supra-/infrahyoid neck
Breast; liver; prostate only
Only temporal bone and thyroid
Only head trauma and sinuses

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR study guide names orbit, sinonasal cavity/facial bones, skull base including sella, CPA/IAC, temporal bone, suprahyoid and infrahyoid neck.

practiceQuestions.stem: When using the TCIA HNSCC collection in an educational exercise, what restriction is specifically important?

options.text: Some images may allow facial reconstruction and may fall under NIH controlled-data access policy
Images are synthetic and need no citation
Data can be rehosted without terms
Clinical metadata is guaranteed complete

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA states the collection is authentic human imaging and de-identified, but some images could reconstruct a face; follow current access/use conditions and data citation.

title: Ophthalmic Plastic Surgery Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship curriculum (independent self-study; not institutional training)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced medical learner; intended for ophthalmology residents/fellows or physicians with prior ophthalmic examination knowledge; not for unsupervised clinical use.
Know ocular anatomy, visual acuity/pupil/motility exam, basic CT/MRI concepts and clinical evidence appraisal.
This independent course is not a prerequisite or substitute for ACGME residency/fellowship.
objectives: Perform structured written reasoning on eyelid, orbit and lacrimal presentations using examination, anatomy and appropriate imaging.
Recognize urgent vision-threatening conditions and formulate escalation priorities without asserting independent procedural competence.
Develop differentials for ptosis, proptosis, eyelid lesions, epiphora, malposition and exposure using red flags and uncertainty.
Interpret broad ACGME subspecialty competency expectations while distinguishing training standards from a public exam blueprint.
Appraise free sources and case images with copyright, patient privacy, consent and evidentiary limits in mind.
Distinguish ABO ophthalmology board certification from ASOPRS society membership exams and institutional fellowship training.

units.title: Clinical foundations: anatomy, examination and documentation
objectives: Relate eyelid, lacrimal, orbital and facial anatomy to symptoms and examination.
Build a structured, safety-oriented oculofacial examination including acuity, pupils, motility, globe position, lid margin and ocular surface.
Document uncertainty and red flags without overcalling a diagnosis.
topics: Eyelid/orbit/lacrimal anatomy; external examination; MRD1, levator function, brow position, Hertel comparison; pupils, color, motility, ocular surface; consent and photo standards.
boardDomains: ACGME core anatomy/examination; ABO general ophthalmology clinical reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: contrast pseudoptosis, dermatochalasis, ptosis and proptosis using a written exam template.
units.assessment: Submit a structured exam note; rubric 40% completeness, 30% localization, 20% safety/red flags, 10% uncertainty/communication.

units.title: Orbital imaging and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Select CT, MRI, ultrasound or no imaging according to clinical question and urgency.
Recognize bone, sinus, muscle, lacrimal gland, optic nerve and orbital apex patterns while preserving differential diagnosis.
topics: Trauma CT; contrast CT for infection/mass; MRI soft-tissue/nerve/inflammatory workup; ultrasound role/limits; artifact and urgent escalation.
boardDomains: ACGME imaging competency; ABO written/oral clinical reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: make a modality-choice matrix for bony trauma, suspected abscess, orbital mass and apical neuropathy.
units.assessment: Imaging memo; rubric 35% modality rationale, 35% differential, 20% urgency, 10% limitations.

units.title: Oculofacial emergency triage: orbital compartment syndrome and infection
objectives: Identify time-critical vision- and life-threatening orbital presentations.
Explain why treatment of clinically suspected compartment syndrome should not await imaging.
Differentiate preseptal from postseptal disease and escalate suspected invasive infection.
topics: OCS signs and clinical diagnosis; traumatic and nontraumatic causes; red flags; orbital cellulitis/abscess; sinus and intracranial risk; team escalation.
boardDomains: ACGME patient care and imaging; ABO oral reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: sort fictional vignettes into immediate emergency escalation, urgent specialist review or routine workup.
units.assessment: Triage oral-board station; rubric 40% recognition, 30% appropriate urgency, 20% no imaging delay in OCS, 10% communication.

units.title: Orbital and periocular trauma
objectives: Use history, ocular examination and imaging to identify globe, optic nerve, orbital and lacrimal risks.
Discuss fracture patterns and avoid equating radiographic fracture alone with an automatic indication for operation.
topics: Blunt/penetrating periocular trauma; fracture; entrapment vs edema; foreign bodies; laceration/anatomical landmark injury; post-traumatic diplopia; compartment syndrome.
boardDomains: ACGME orbital imaging/examination; ABO trauma reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: review published EyeRounds trauma cases by link; create a differential and missing-data list; no image capture.
units.assessment: Case analysis; rubric 30% exam priorities, 30% imaging choice, 25% differential/urgency, 15% consent/privacy.

units.title: Thyroid eye disease and orbital inflammatory disease
objectives: Classify TED activity and severity using current standardized frameworks.
Distinguish TED from orbital myositis, IgG4-related disease, neoplasm and infection using clinical/imaging pattern plus caveats.
Recognize sight-threatening optic neuropathy or corneal compromise as urgent.
topics: CAS limits; severity and progression; thyroid status/smoking; CT/MRI patterns; multidisciplinary treatment selection; sight-threatening disease; stable-phase rehabilitation sequencing.
boardDomains: ACGME orbital anatomy/imaging; ABO reasoning; no separate published ASOPRS blueprint available publicly
units.casePractice: Case practice: apply CAS/severity rubric to fictional cases; state what evidence would change the plan.
units.assessment: TED decision memo; rubric 30% activity/severity, 30% urgent threats, 25% differential, 15% evidence/date qualification.

units.title: Lacrimal system and acquired obstruction
objectives: Interpret lacrimal history and examination, including irrigation outcomes and reflux, within differential diagnosis.
Identify cases needing imaging/endoscopy or urgent referral rather than assuming uncomplicated obstruction.
Compare external and endoscopic DCR as options without giving a procedural competency claim.
topics: Punctal/canalicular/sac/duct anatomy; epiphora; PANDO; dacryocystitis; congenital vs acquired; trauma/tumor warning features; DCR approaches and multidisciplinary care.
boardDomains: ACGME lacrimal exam; ABO reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: trace causes of epiphora and state when reflux/patency is informative; use published dacryocystitis case only by link.
units.assessment: Lacrimal referral note; rubric 35% localization, 25% differential, 25% appropriate tests/referral, 15% limits.

units.title: Eyelid malposition, ptosis and brow
objectives: Distinguish true ptosis, pseudoptosis, dermatochalasis, retraction, entropion, ectropion and brow ptosis.
Use laterality, pupils, motility, onset and levator function to identify neurogenic or myogenic concerns.
Explain function, ocular-surface and aesthetic considerations of management.
topics: MRD1/levator function; Horner/third nerve/myasthenic differential; congenital ptosis and amblyopia risk; facial palsy; involutional malposition; exposure.
boardDomains: ACGME exam and ocular surface; ABO oral clinical reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: diagram differential by pupil/motility and construct a measurement table.
units.assessment: Written diagnostic comparison; rubric 35% localization, 35% differential/red flags, 20% objective measures, 10% patient-centered goals.

units.title: Periocular tumors, biopsy logic and pathology
objectives: Recognize warning features in eyelid lesions and describe the role of biopsy/pathology rather than diagnose from appearance alone.
Distinguish common benign lesions from malignancy patterns and identify masquerade/recurrent lesions needing expert evaluation.
Plan multidisciplinary oncologic discussion at a conceptual level.
topics: Basal/squamous/sebaceous/melanocytic and adnexal lesions; margin architecture/lash loss; recurrence; map biopsies as relevant; histopathology and pathology correlation.
boardDomains: ACGME ocular/cutaneous pathology requirement including slide review; ABO clinical judgment
units.casePractice: Case practice: compare a recurrent “chalazion” with a changing lesion; list biopsy/pathology questions; no diagnosis from synthetic images.
units.assessment: Lesion risk stratification memo; rubric 30% red flags, 30% differential, 25% tissue/pathology logic, 15% uncertainty/referral.

units.title: Orbital neoplasia and inflammatory mimics
objectives: Organize proptosis/mass differential by tempo, age, pain, laterality and compartment.
Choose imaging and biopsy/referral questions while recognizing limitations and emergencies.
topics: Lymphoproliferative, vascular, lacrimal gland and neural lesions; idiopathic orbital inflammation; IgG4-related disease; infection; optic neuropathy; staging collaboration.
boardDomains: ACGME regional anatomy/pathology/imaging; ABO reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: build a proptosis localization/differential tree; use the EyeRounds collection by link only.
units.assessment: Differential map; rubric 30% localization, 30% imaging choice, 25% alternative diagnoses, 15% escalation.

units.title: Ocular surface, exposure and reconstruction principles
objectives: Connect lid position, facial nerve function, scar and midface/brow to corneal exposure.
Recognize sight-threatening epithelial breakdown and frame protective strategies/referral.
Explain reconstructive options at a conceptual level without procedural instruction.
topics: Lagophthalmos; facial nerve palsy; cicatricial change; corneal exposure; graft donor-site anatomy; staged reconstruction; interdisciplinary care.
boardDomains: ACGME ocular surface, regional anatomy, wound healing; ABO patient-care reasoning
units.casePractice: Case practice: map cause→exposure risk→protective goal for facial palsy/TED/cicatricial scenarios.
units.assessment: Exposure risk plan; rubric 35% mechanism, 30% urgent corneal risk, 20% team/referral, 15% limits.

units.title: Aesthetic surgery, ethics and perioperative safety
objectives: Elicit patient goals and distinguish functional from elective cosmetic concerns.
Discuss risk, expectation-setting, consent, complications and patient safety in a culturally responsive way.
Identify when uncertainty, ocular surface risk or systemic factors should defer elective decisions.
topics: Brow/lid relationships; functional documentation; perioperative assessment; asymmetry; informed consent; image privacy; bias/access; complications and follow-up.
boardDomains: ACGME communication, professionalism and systems-based practice; ABO oral judgment
units.casePractice: Case practice: write a shared-decision conversation for a fictional elective referral with competing functional/aesthetic goals.
units.assessment: Consent and communication exercise; rubric 30% patient goals, 30% risks/alternatives, 20% equitable language, 20% documentation.

units.title: Integration, evidence appraisal and ASOPRS membership exam context
objectives: Integrate anatomy, examination, imaging, pathology and patient goals in a defensible differential.
Appraise evidence limits and distinguish ACGME training requirements, ABO board certification, and ASOPRS society membership.
Develop a self-directed study and scholarly question plan without claiming exam readiness.
topics: Case synthesis; ACGME competency framework; scholarly activity/thesis; ASOPRS written/oral entrance exams; ABO written/oral primary-board process; privacy/consent.
boardDomains: ACGME competencies; ABO examination; ASOPRS membership path; no public ASOPRS blueprint
units.casePractice: Case practice: do a timed fictional multi-domain oral case, record assumptions and missing facts; no actual exam content.
units.assessment: Integrated case viva and evidence critique; rubric 30% prioritization, 25% differential, 20% evidence quality, 15% uncertainty, 10% professional limits.

assignment.title: Integrated oculofacial case conference dossier
assignment.instructions: Prepare a 1,500–2,000-word analysis of three linked fictional vignettes (acute proptosis after trauma; acquired tearing; recurrent eyelid lesion). Use no generated diagnostic image and no copied patient image. Include triage priorities, missing information, structured examination, imaging rationale, differential, evidence citations, referral/escalation and a rights/privacy audit of any linked public case resource. Do not write patient-specific treatment advice.

unitMap.text: Clinical foundations: anatomy, examination and documentation
coveredTopics: Eyelid/orbit/lacrimal anatomy; external examination; MRD1, levator function, brow position, Hertel comparison; pupils, color, motility, ocular surface; consent and photo standards.

unitMap.text: Orbital imaging and diagnostic reasoning
coveredTopics: Trauma CT; contrast CT for infection/mass; MRI soft-tissue/nerve/inflammatory workup; ultrasound role/limits; artifact and urgent escalation.

unitMap.text: Oculofacial emergency triage: orbital compartment syndrome and infection
coveredTopics: OCS signs and clinical diagnosis; traumatic and nontraumatic causes; red flags; orbital cellulitis/abscess; sinus and intracranial risk; team escalation.

unitMap.text: Orbital and periocular trauma
coveredTopics: Blunt/penetrating periocular trauma; fracture; entrapment vs edema; foreign bodies; laceration/anatomical landmark injury; post-traumatic diplopia; compartment syndrome.

unitMap.text: Thyroid eye disease and orbital inflammatory disease
coveredTopics: CAS limits; severity and progression; thyroid status/smoking; CT/MRI patterns; multidisciplinary treatment selection; sight-threatening disease; stable-phase rehabilitation sequencing.

unitMap.text: Lacrimal system and acquired obstruction
coveredTopics: Punctal/canalicular/sac/duct anatomy; epiphora; PANDO; dacryocystitis; congenital vs acquired; trauma/tumor warning features; DCR approaches and multidisciplinary care.

unitMap.text: Eyelid malposition, ptosis and brow
coveredTopics: MRD1/levator function; Horner/third nerve/myasthenic differential; congenital ptosis and amblyopia risk; facial palsy; involutional malposition; exposure.

unitMap.text: Periocular tumors, biopsy logic and pathology
coveredTopics: Basal/squamous/sebaceous/melanocytic and adnexal lesions; margin architecture/lash loss; recurrence; map biopsies as relevant; histopathology and pathology correlation.

unitMap.text: Orbital neoplasia and inflammatory mimics
coveredTopics: Lymphoproliferative, vascular, lacrimal gland and neural lesions; idiopathic orbital inflammation; IgG4-related disease; infection; optic neuropathy; staging collaboration.

unitMap.text: Ocular surface, exposure and reconstruction principles
coveredTopics: Lagophthalmos; facial nerve palsy; cicatricial change; corneal exposure; graft donor-site anatomy; staged reconstruction; interdisciplinary care.

unitMap.text: Aesthetic surgery, ethics and perioperative safety
coveredTopics: Brow/lid relationships; functional documentation; perioperative assessment; asymmetry; informed consent; image privacy; bias/access; complications and follow-up.

unitMap.text: Integration, evidence appraisal and ASOPRS membership exam context
coveredTopics: Case synthesis; ACGME competency framework; scholarly activity/thesis; ASOPRS written/oral entrance exams; ABO written/oral primary-board process; privacy/consent.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with recent facial trauma has progressive proptosis, a tense orbit, reduced acuity and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Which action principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Obtain MRI before any intervention
Treat suspected orbital compartment syndrome as a clinical emergency; do not delay decompression for imaging
Observe until swelling resolves
A visible orbital fracture excludes compartment syndrome

practiceQuestions.rationale: OCS is a clinical diagnosis; delay for imaging risks irreversible ischemia. A fracture does not exclude OCS. This is an educational principle, not a procedural credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: An orbital CT is requested after blunt trauma. Which question is CT particularly useful for answering?

options.text: Fine soft-tissue characterization of optic nerve inflammation
Orbital bone fracture and suspected foreign body localization
Excluding all soft-tissue orbital disease
Measuring lacrimal drainage flow

practiceQuestions.rationale: CT is particularly useful for bony trauma and foreign bodies; MRI provides better soft-tissue characterization in selected nonemergent settings.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with Graves disease has new reduction in acuity and worsening color desaturation with apical crowding. What is the best educational priority?

options.text: Routine cosmetic evaluation
Urgent assessment for sight-threatening TED and specialist multidisciplinary management
Defer assessment until disease is inactive
Assume all TED responds identically to one drug

practiceQuestions.rationale: Suspected dysthyroid optic neuropathy is sight-threatening and requires urgent specialist assessment; current guidance stratifies disease by activity, severity and duration.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an adult with persistent epiphora, irrigation through the lacrimal system refluxes from the opposite punctum. Which interpretation is most consistent with Harvard Eye Insights?

options.text: The system is patent
This supports obstruction; localize and consider referral/workup
It proves a congenital defect
It is diagnostic of orbital tumor

practiceQuestions.rationale: Contralateral punctal reflux during irrigation indicates obstruction in the relevant drainage pathway; additional workup is guided by context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A long-standing “chalazion” recurs and the eyelid margin shows focal lash loss and architectural destruction. What is the most appropriate reasoning?

options.text: Reassure because all recurrent eyelid lumps are benign
Consider malignancy in the differential and seek appropriate specialist/pathologic evaluation
Treat appearance as diagnostic of sebaceous carcinoma
Avoid tissue diagnosis in all cases

practiceQuestions.rationale: Recurrent lesion and margin disruption are concerning features but are not by themselves diagnostic; pathology and clinical assessment matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child presents with ptosis. Which data are particularly important before discussing management?

options.text: Pupil examination, motility, onset/history, visual development/amblyopia risk, and ptosis measurements
Only cosmetic preference
Only CT of both orbits
No examination if congenital

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric ptosis evaluation must consider etiology and visual development, including amblyopia risk; sudden onset, anisocoria or motility abnormalities alter urgency/differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with facial nerve palsy has incomplete eyelid closure and corneal staining. What is the key oculoplastic concept?

options.text: Lid position and facial function can threaten the ocular surface; assess severity and arrange timely protective care
Exposure is always benign
Imaging is the only useful assessment
Elective cosmetic correction is the first priority

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME requirements emphasize ocular surface pathology and how lids, midface and brow contribute to exposure; corneal compromise requires attention.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes ASOPRS exams from ABO certification?

options.text: ASOPRS entrance exams are a legally required state medical license
ASOPRS written/oral exams plus thesis relate to society membership; ABO examinations confer ophthalmology board certification
ASOPRS membership is automatically board certification
The fellowship itself grants an independent board certificate

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASOPRS publishes thesis and written/oral membership requirements. ABO separately describes its two-step board-certification examinations after accredited ophthalmology residency.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has painless unilateral lacrimal gland enlargement and proptosis. Which principle best guides the next step?

options.text: Assume TED without examining other causes
Localize and characterize the orbital process with appropriate imaging and differential; consider inflammatory, lymphoproliferative and neoplastic causes
Use CT and MRI interchangeably in every case
Do not seek tissue diagnosis under any circumstances

practiceQuestions.rationale: Orbital masses have broad differential diagnoses; CT/MRI choice depends on anatomy and question; specialist-directed diagnostic workup is required.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the free EyeRounds oculoplastic video catalogue?

options.text: It is a 36-hour fellowship lecture course
It contains many short examination and technique videos, so runtime alone does not make them lecture hours
It authorizes unrestricted rehosting of patient images
It provides supervised surgical privileges

practiceQuestions.rationale: EyeRounds lists numerous short procedural demonstrations, typically seconds to minutes; this curriculum excludes them from substantive lecture-hour totals. Its published policy limits image reuse and requires consent in specified circumstances.

title: Cornea Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent self-study curriculum; not a clinical training programme)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Licensed/qualified physician with completed ophthalmology residency or equivalent background; this course does not establish that status.
Comfort with ocular anatomy, slit-lamp findings, refraction, anterior-segment imaging, microbiology, evidence appraisal and ophthalmology clinical reasoning.
Learners without clinical ophthalmology training should use patient-facing material only under appropriate professional supervision; not as self-care or practice instruction.
objectives: Integrate corneal anatomy and optics with anterior-segment examination and imaging.
Generate a differential for infectious, inflammatory, degenerative, dystrophic, ectatic, traumatic and ocular-surface disorders.
Interpret topography, tomography, pachymetry and anterior-segment imaging while stating technical and diagnostic limitations.
Apply evidence-informed reasoning to keratoconus progression, contact-lens rehabilitation, CXL and keratoplasty selection concepts.
Compare PK, DALK, DSAEK and DMEK by anatomy, indications, trade-offs and major complications.
Recognize corneal emergencies and the need for prompt specialist assessment; no individual treatment instructions.
Explain eye-bank, donor-tissue, consent, postoperative surveillance and multidisciplinary considerations at a conceptual level.
Evaluate authentic open case resources lawfully, without copying or rehosting patient images or records.

units.title: Corneal anatomy, optics, examination and documentation
objectives: Relate epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Descemet membrane, endothelium and limbus to signs of disease.
Build an anterior-segment examination and describe visual function beyond acuity.
Select photography, pachymetry, topography/tomography, AS-OCT, specular microscopy and confocal microscopy by question.
topics: Slit-lamp localization; tear film and surface assessment; refraction; staining; corneal sensation; IOP; test limitations.
boardDomains: Ophthalmology: cornea/external disease foundations; no independently verified weighted ABO blueprint was available.
units.casePractice: Use a licensed/open case page only as a link; practice a structured note from one open EyeRounds case.
units.assessment: 5-domain rubric: anatomy 20%, interpretation 25%, test selection 20%, limitations 20%, clear note 15%.

units.title: Ocular surface, tear film and dry eye
objectives: Classify aqueous, evaporative and mixed dry-eye mechanisms without assuming one test is diagnostic.
Recognize exposure, neurotrophic, medication toxicity and cicatrizing disease in persistent defects.
Sequence nonprocedural management concepts and identify when specialist coordination is needed.
topics: Tear film/lids/meibomian glands; staining; exposure; neurotrophic disease; cicatrizing disease; scleral and bandage lenses; serum tears and amniotic membrane (evidence/risks).
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; ocular-surface systems.
units.casePractice: Compare two published surface cases; identify competing etiologies and surface findings.
units.assessment: Differential 25%, evidence use 25%, safe escalation 25%, concise documentation 25%.

units.title: Infectious keratitis: urgent assessment and bacterial disease
objectives: Distinguish ulceration as a finding from confirmed microbial infection.
Use risk, size, location, stromal depth, atypical features and response to prioritize microbiology and referral.
Explain culture, smear and molecular-test roles and empiric-treatment principles without dosing directives.
topics: Bacterial keratitis; contact lens risks; scrape/culture indications; susceptibility; serial measurements; referral/escalation.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; emergency assessment.
units.casePractice: Analyze public case resources; explain what features raise concern and what additional data are needed.
units.assessment: Risk-stratification 30%, diagnostic plan 30%, evidence/caveats 20%, communication 20%.

units.title: Fungal, Acanthamoeba, viral and atypical keratitis
objectives: Construct a differential from history, exposure, phenotype, layer and trajectory.
Recognize why appearance alone does not establish organism.
Explain limitations of PCR, culture and confocal tests; distinguish epithelial from stromal/endothelial viral involvement conceptually.
topics: Fungal keratitis; Acanthamoeba; HSV/VZV; atypical bacteria; mixed disease; immunosuppression and steroid cautions.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; infectious differential diagnosis.
units.casePractice: Compare the published EyeRounds Acanthamoeba, Fusarium and HSV cases without treating a photograph as a definitive test.
units.assessment: Differential 30%, test limitations 25%, urgency 25%, source-grounding 20%.

units.title: Corneal dystrophies, degenerations, scars and edema
objectives: Organize inherited dystrophies by layer and distinguish them from degenerations and secondary opacities.
Interpret symptoms, slit-lamp morphology and functional change in Fuchs endothelial dystrophy.
Use history, imaging and serial change to distinguish edema from opacity/scar and assess transplant need.
topics: EBMD, stromal dystrophies, Fuchs, posterior polymorphous dystrophy, band keratopathy, Salzmann, neurotrophic opacity, edema.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; anterior-segment differential.
units.casePractice: Make a morphology-to-layer map using NEI, AAO PPP and Iowa case links.
units.assessment: Layer localization 30%, differential 25%, functional interpretation 20%, evidence 25%.

units.title: Corneal ectasia and keratoconus: detection and risk assessment
objectives: Interpret topography and tomography as complementary rather than interchangeable tests.
Recognize anterior/posterior elevation and thickness-distribution patterns and contact-lens confounding.
Describe progression as change across more than one relevant domain; counsel on uncertainty.
topics: Keratoconus; pellucid marginal degeneration; post-refractive ectasia; epithelial mapping; posterior elevation; tomography; contact-lens abstinence.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; refractive surgery safety.
units.casePractice: Review Iowa keratoconus cases and create a one-page imaging differential, without copied images.
units.assessment: Pattern 30%, confounders 20%, progression reasoning 30%, clarity 20%.

units.title: Keratoconus: stabilization and visual rehabilitation
objectives: Compare observation, specialty contact lenses, CXL, intracorneal support and keratoplasty by clinical goal.
Explain CXL as a progression-stabilizing option, not a guarantee of reversal.
Compare DALK and PK when endothelium is healthy versus involved.
topics: Risk reduction/eye rubbing; CXL; contact lens rehab; rings/CAIRS; hydrops; DALK/PK selection.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; ectasia management; refractive risk.
units.casePractice: Write a decision memo for a fictional progressing-ectasia vignette, stating what missing evidence changes the plan.
units.assessment: Options and indications 30%, evidence 25%, alternatives 20%, uncertainty/safety 25%.

units.title: Corneal imaging and refractive surgery
objectives: Explain what Placido topography, Scheimpflug tomography, AS-OCT, pachymetry and epithelial maps measure.
Identify ectasia risk factors and limitations in preoperative screening.
Contrast PRK, LASIK and SMILE risk concepts without promising safety for any individual.
topics: Corneal shape/optics; ectasia screening; refractive procedure selection; post-LASIK ectasia; post-op complications.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; refractive surgery; imaging.
units.casePractice: Prepare a refractive-surgery screening checklist and explain why an unstable refraction warrants deferral/assessment.
units.assessment: Modality matching 25%, risk identification 30%, limitation statements 25%, communication 20%.

units.title: Corneal transplantation: donor tissue and procedure selection
objectives: Choose the transplant question by the diseased layer and visual/tectonic goals.
Compare PK, DALK, DSAEK/DSEK and DMEK anatomy, indications, trade-offs and major failure modes.
Discuss tissue/eye-bank, consent, donor safety and access considerations.
topics: PK; DALK; DSAEK; DMEK; keratoprosthesis; therapeutic versus optical graft; eye-bank tissue.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; transplant surgery concepts.
units.casePractice: Create a procedure comparison from the University of Iowa tutorial; cite rather than reproduce its diagrams.
units.assessment: Layer/procedure match 35%, trade-offs 25%, alternatives 20%, citation 20%.

units.title: Endothelial keratoplasty and Fuchs surgery planning
objectives: Explain donor/host tissue distinction for DSAEK vs DMEK.
Identify graft adherence, detachment, rebubbling and pressure concerns conceptually.
Account for corneal shape change, cataract and IOL planning, and functional expectations.
topics: Fuchs; pseudophakic bullous keratopathy; DMEK/DSAEK; combined/sequential surgery; hyperopic shift; graft attachment.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; cataract and anterior-segment interfaces.
units.casePractice: Compare the Fuchs/EK published cases; outline which anatomy and visual data must be known before selecting approach.
units.assessment: Technique comparison 30%, imaging 20%, complications 25%, source-aware caveat 25%.

units.title: PK/DALK surgery, complications and postoperative care
objectives: Map indications and major anatomical differences in full-thickness and lamellar keratoplasty.
Recognize graft infection, wound problems, epithelial defects, glaucoma, rejection and failure as distinct complications.
Explain the need for lifelong surveillance and rapid evaluation of new graft symptoms without directing self-treatment.
topics: Donor selection; suture/astigmatism concepts; wound integrity; rejection vs failure; IOP; epithelial healing; follow-up.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; post-op complication recognition.
units.casePractice: Use Iowa’s public tutorials as links only and construct a complication time-course matrix.
units.assessment: Complication recognition 35%, differential 25%, follow-up logic 20%, caveats 20%.

units.title: Ocular surface failure, limbal stem-cell deficiency and reconstruction
objectives: Recognize patterns of limbal stem-cell deficiency and common acquired causes.
Explain why the underlying surface/inflammation and lids must be addressed before optical graft expectations.
Compare autologous/allogeneic reconstruction at a conceptual level, including immunosuppression/team risks.
topics: Chemical/thermal injury; SJS/OCP; contact lens or medication toxicity; limbal grafts; AMT; keratoprosthesis; multidisciplinary care.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; ocular surface reconstruction.
units.casePractice: Write a staged reconstruction discussion for a fictional case, explicitly separating what is unknown from confirmed.
units.assessment: Cause/stage reasoning 30%, sequence 25%, risk/team 25%, limits 20%.

units.title: Pediatric cornea and congenital opacity
objectives: Build age-sensitive differentials for congenital and childhood corneal opacity.
Explain amblyopia/visual-development implications and need for pediatric/multidisciplinary assessment.
Compare pediatric donor/timing/rehabilitation questions without making a surgical recommendation.
topics: Peters anomaly; congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy; birth trauma/infection; pediatric keratoconus; visual development.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; pediatric ophthalmology collaboration.
units.casePractice: Review a public Iowa pediatric case and list phenotype, age, systemic history and missing work-up.
units.assessment: Differential 30%, developmental context 25%, missing data 25%, clarity 20%.

units.title: Corneal refractive surgery and postoperative ectasia
objectives: Explain procedure-dependent biomechanical tissue alteration conceptually.
Use pre-op stability and multimodal imaging to flag risk; distinguish planned treatment from complication.
Recognize that CXL has limits in post-refractive ectasia and that disease course needs follow-up.
topics: LASIK/PRK/SMILE; ectasia risk; enhancement; topography/tomography; interface complications; post-op care.
boardDomains: Cornea/external disease; refractive surgery.
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional preoperative screening record and write a stop/seek-further-evaluation rationale.
units.assessment: Risk flags 35%, imaging 25%, alternatives 20%, non-overclaim 20%.

units.title: Research literacy, outcomes, professionalism and board-style synthesis
objectives: Critically appraise case series, guideline recommendations, endpoints and conflicts.
Use licensing and privacy rules to access authentic educational cases responsibly.
Integrate a multi-domain corneal case in a structured oral reasoning response.
topics: AUPO fellowship learning objectives; evidence hierarchy; patient safety; human factors; referral; consent; image rights.
boardDomains: ABO general ophthalmology knowledge/judgment; not a cornea certification blueprint.
units.casePractice: Deliver a 10-minute source-cited case conference using one public case URL; do not reproduce case images or patient records.
units.assessment: Reasoning 30%, evidence 25%, patient safety and limits 25%, oral clarity 20%.

assignment.name: Corneal case conference and evidence portfolio

components.name: Case reasoning brief
components.deliverable: 1,000–1,500 words; source-cited analysis of an authentic linked educational case, no image copied. Identify key findings, differential, missing information, test limitations, urgency and reasonable referral questions.

components.name: Imaging and layer map
components.deliverable: Original diagram or prose matching corneal layer to diagnostic modalities and procedure concepts; no copied scans.

components.name: Transplant comparison memo
components.deliverable: Compare PK/DALK/DSAEK/DMEK according to affected layer, scarring, endothelial status, optical/tectonic goal and uncertainty.

components.name: Board-style question set
components.deliverable: Answer course-authored items with rationales and citations; questions are not official ABO items.

components.name: Professionalism and media-rights statement
components.deliverable: Document access status, licensing restrictions and why public-viewable images are linked rather than reproduced.

rubric: Patient safety, referral and credential boundaries 15%
assignment.grading: Educational formative grading only; suggested proficiency threshold 80% for internal course completion, not an exam pass predictor.

assessment.format: 10 original single-best-answer questions plus 5 portfolio assignments.
assessment.scorePlan: Question bank 20%, assignments 80%; use assignment rubrics above.
assessment.completionNote: No validated relationship between this assessment, ABO results, clinical competence or surgical outcomes. No official exam questions are included.

studyHours.note: Transparent learner study plan only, not a claim about the MEE fellowship’s didactic hours. The 74-hour nonvideo allocation covers linked readings, case reasoning, image interpretation, assignments and review. Video production plans are separate and not counted as ready hours.

mapping.name: MEE Cornea Fellowship — one-year option (SF Match #4253)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a one-year Cornea, External Disease, and Refractive Surgery fellowship; about 90% of time is clinical care with remaining time available for research. Fellows see outpatient and emergency cases, perform under supervision, attend lectures, and present cases. AUPO-FCC-certified; this is a statement about program compliance, not a board certificate. Public page lists 1–2 fellows/year.

mapping.name: MEE Cornea Fellowship — two-year option (SF Match #4292)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page lists this two-year match route and number #4292. Publicly extracted page does not explain how its curriculum differs from the one-year route; no difference is inferred.

unitMap.text: Corneal anatomy, optics, examination and documentation
coveredTopics: Slit-lamp localization; tear film and surface assessment; refraction; staining; corneal sensation; IOP; test limitations.

unitMap.text: Ocular surface, tear film and dry eye
coveredTopics: Tear film/lids/meibomian glands; staining; exposure; neurotrophic disease; cicatrizing disease; scleral and bandage lenses; serum tears and amniotic membrane (evidence/risks).

unitMap.text: Infectious keratitis: urgent assessment and bacterial disease
coveredTopics: Bacterial keratitis; contact lens risks; scrape/culture indications; susceptibility; serial measurements; referral/escalation.

unitMap.text: Fungal, Acanthamoeba, viral and atypical keratitis
coveredTopics: Fungal keratitis; Acanthamoeba; HSV/VZV; atypical bacteria; mixed disease; immunosuppression and steroid cautions.

unitMap.text: Corneal dystrophies, degenerations, scars and edema
coveredTopics: EBMD, stromal dystrophies, Fuchs, posterior polymorphous dystrophy, band keratopathy, Salzmann, neurotrophic opacity, edema.

unitMap.text: Corneal ectasia and keratoconus: detection and risk assessment
coveredTopics: Keratoconus; pellucid marginal degeneration; post-refractive ectasia; epithelial mapping; posterior elevation; tomography; contact-lens abstinence.

unitMap.text: Keratoconus: stabilization and visual rehabilitation
coveredTopics: Risk reduction/eye rubbing; CXL; contact lens rehab; rings/CAIRS; hydrops; DALK/PK selection.

unitMap.text: Corneal imaging and refractive surgery
coveredTopics: Corneal shape/optics; ectasia screening; refractive procedure selection; post-LASIK ectasia; post-op complications.

unitMap.text: Corneal transplantation: donor tissue and procedure selection
coveredTopics: PK; DALK; DSAEK; DMEK; keratoprosthesis; therapeutic versus optical graft; eye-bank tissue.

unitMap.text: Endothelial keratoplasty and Fuchs surgery planning
coveredTopics: Fuchs; pseudophakic bullous keratopathy; DMEK/DSAEK; combined/sequential surgery; hyperopic shift; graft attachment.

unitMap.text: PK/DALK surgery, complications and postoperative care
coveredTopics: Donor selection; suture/astigmatism concepts; wound integrity; rejection vs failure; IOP; epithelial healing; follow-up.

unitMap.text: Ocular surface failure, limbal stem-cell deficiency and reconstruction
coveredTopics: Chemical/thermal injury; SJS/OCP; contact lens or medication toxicity; limbal grafts; AMT; keratoprosthesis; multidisciplinary care.

unitMap.text: Pediatric cornea and congenital opacity
coveredTopics: Peters anomaly; congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy; birth trauma/infection; pediatric keratoconus; visual development.

unitMap.text: Corneal refractive surgery and postoperative ectasia
coveredTopics: LASIK/PRK/SMILE; ectasia risk; enhancement; topography/tomography; interface complications; post-op care.

unitMap.text: Research literacy, outcomes, professionalism and board-style synthesis
coveredTopics: AUPO fellowship learning objectives; evidence hierarchy; patient safety; human factors; referral; consent; image rights.

topicGaps: The ≥36-hour verified-recording floor is met by unique public media IDs with observed runtimes. This count does not establish board readiness, clinical competence, or hours of supervised training; accessible recordings are not guaranteed to remain available.
No official weighted ABO cornea-specific examination blueprint was identified. Unit/domain mapping remains qualitative ophthalmology study alignment, not a formal cornea board blueprint.

The MEE public page describes clinical rotations and educational activities but does not publish a complete lecture schedule, case/procedure counts, or the curriculum difference between its SF Match #4253 one-year and #4292 two-year options.

Pediatric congenital opacity and corneal genetics are less developed than adult disease and transplantation; the pediatric transplant recording does not replace pediatric ophthalmology/genetics supervision.

Keratoprosthesis selection, long-term device surveillance, eye-bank tissue policy, consent, and current evidence for surface reconstruction need deeper clinician-verified source teaching than the current public lecture ledger provides.
Several supplemental recorded lectures are older (2017–2022); learner and clinician review must check current practice, local resources, and guideline updates before use.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

officialProgrammes.name: MEE Cornea Fellowship — one-year option (SF Match #4253)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a one-year Cornea, External Disease, and Refractive Surgery fellowship; about 90% of time is clinical care with remaining time available for research. medical.programmeSourceScope: Official Mass General Brigham listing plus official AUPO FCC subspecialty scope/requirements. MEE states that fellows treat complex anterior-segment disease, participate in corneal/refractive surgery, provide consults/emergency coverage, and attend lectures/conferences. Its public page is a programme description, not a full lecture syllabus. ACGME requirements page covers ophthalmology residency and is not treated as a cornea fellowship accreditation standard. AUPO FCC compliance is distinguished from ACGME accreditation and ABO certification.
sourceCaveats: No human clinical review was performed. Clinical content must be checked by a qualified cornea specialist before use with patients.
MEE describes itself as an AUPO-FCC-certified clinical fellowship; that does not mean the self-study course is affiliated, accredited, or itself compliant.

ABO public pages retrieved identify ophthalmology board examinations and eligibility after residency. No separate cornea-specific ABO examination was identified; this is not a claim that no other voluntary, non-board certificate exists. The ABO eligibility page was not readable in the retrieval session; users must consult the live eligibility rules.
No official weighted cornea-specific ABO exam blueprint was retrieved. Unit mappings are qualitative study alignment, not a claim of formal board blueprint alignment or exam readiness.
Public MEE curricula do not disclose every lecture, clinical case, procedure count, or two-year-route differences. No patient volume or surgical competency is inferred.
Publicly viewable clinical images are not copied. License status may differ by page; link only and obtain permission for any reuse.
External media runtimes and availability can change. Counts reflect public metadata and pages observed on 2026-10-07; recheck before delivery/use.
Free public recorded lectures are self-study resources, not peer-reviewed lectures in every claim, official MEE content, or supervised procedure training.

This independent curriculum grants no Harvard/MEE affiliation, accredited training, clinical privileges, licensure, radiation/clinical authorization, board eligibility, procedure competence, certification, or guarantee of passing any examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: A candidate for keratorefractive surgery reports fluctuating refraction while recently wearing contact lenses. Which next step best matches current corneal ectasia guidance?

options.text: Use corrected acuity alone to clear surgery.
Allow a period of contact-lens abstinence, then assess topography and tomography for irregularity or ectasia.
Assume normal central pachymetry excludes ectasia.
Proceed because PRK and SMILE have zero ectasia risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO guidance says to evaluate for ectasia after a period of contact lens abstinence and review topography/tomography. Acuity or a single thickness measure is insufficient; lower comparative risk is not zero risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most accurate general goal of corneal collagen cross-linking in progressive keratoconus?

options.text: Guaranteed restoration of normal corneal shape and acuity.
Stabilization that reduces risk of progression; visual rehabilitation may still require lenses or other care.
Replacement of diseased endothelium.
Treatment that eliminates all future need for follow-up.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO PPP describes CXL as stabilizing progressive keratoconus and reducing progressive ectasia risk. It does not promise reversal, normal vision, or eliminate monitoring.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational vignette describes ectasia with stromal scarring absent and a healthy endothelium. Which graft concept selectively replaces diseased anterior stroma while preserving host endothelium?

options.text: DALK
DMEK
DSAEK
PK is the only possible approach

practiceQuestions.rationale: DALK replaces anterior stromal tissue and keeps host Descemet membrane/endothelium. Selection depends on actual anatomy and patient factors; this item tests layer-to-procedure reasoning, not candidacy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A middle-aged patient reports morning blur that improves later in the day; slit-lamp examination shows central guttae and corneal edema. Which disease process is most consistent with this pattern?

options.text: Endothelial dysfunction such as Fuchs dystrophy
Isolated superficial epithelial basement membrane irregularity only
Keratoconus progression by definition
Acute angle closure in every case

practiceQuestions.rationale: NEI notes Fuchs endothelial dystrophy can cause endothelial dysfunction, edema and morning blur. Findings require clinical confirmation and differential assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: For endothelial failure without significant stromal scarring, which broad procedural category has largely supplanted PK as the usual tissue-selective concept?

options.text: Endothelial keratoplasty
DALK
Excimer ablation
Intracorneal ring segments

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO edema/opacification PPP states endothelial keratoplasty has supplanted PK when endothelial failure occurs without scarring, with faster visual rehabilitation and less induced astigmatism/rejection risk. Actual choices remain clinician-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which scenario most strongly supports microbiologic testing in a suspected infectious keratitis case?

options.text: A large central infiltrate with deep stromal involvement or melting
A completely resolved superficial abrasion
A stable, asymptomatic normal cornea
No infiltrate, no symptoms and no risk factors

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO bacterial keratitis PPP criteria include central/large infiltrate, substantial stromal involvement or melting, atypical/chronic/unresponsive disease, prior surgery, and multiple infiltrates. Urgent assessment is not delayed to await tests.

practiceQuestions.stem: A corneal infiltrate looks ring-shaped in a contact lens wearer. What is the soundest inference?

options.text: Appearance alone definitively proves Acanthamoeba.
The appearance and exposure inform the differential; microbiology and/or confocal findings may be needed because signs overlap.
A ring means fungal disease only.
Acanthamoeba is excluded if culture is negative.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Infectious keratitis has overlapping presentations. History, clinical examination and tests such as culture/PCR/confocal microscopy contribute; no isolated morphology or negative test always establishes/excludes an organism.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why should a positive molecular test in a corneal scrape be interpreted in clinical context?

options.text: PCR cannot detect microbial genetic material.
It can detect nonviable organisms or contaminants, so a positive result does not by itself prove causation.
PCR replaces all culture and susceptibility testing.
PCR results always identify severity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The review notes PCR can be sensitive but may detect contaminants or nonviable microbial DNA and must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture; culture can provide identification and susceptibility information.

practiceQuestions.stem: A published case shows a central corneal infiltrate in a contact-lens wearer. What is the most defensible educational interpretation?

options.text: It proves a specific pathogen and regimen without history or testing.
It is an authentic teaching clue but must be integrated with history, lesion features, testing, severity and response.
A photograph provides full patient records.
It can be copied into any course because it is publicly viewable.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cases and images inform pattern recognition but cannot independently establish an organism, management, or permissions. Free-to-view is not permission to reproduce or rehost.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about an independent online Cornea Fellowship course and board certification is correct?

options.text: Completing it makes the learner ABO board eligible.
It is self-study only; ABO certification is in ophthalmology and no separate ABO cornea exam was identified.
It grants clinical privileges after the course.
AUPO FCC program compliance is an individual board certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO describes its certification as ophthalmology certification following accredited residency and examinations. AUPO FCC is a fellowship-program compliance process, not an individual cornea board. This independent curriculum confers no eligibility or credential.

unitMap.text: Clinical reasoning, phenotype, and urgent mimics
coveredTopics: age/onset/course, nyctalopia/photophobia, family history and pedigree
acuity, pupils, color, anterior segment, fundus, fields; red flags and referral urgency
avoid anchoring on family history or a single fundus sign

unitMap.text: Inheritance, pedigrees, and counseling
coveredTopics: autosomal dominant/recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial patterns
segregation, phase, variant interpretation limits, cascade testing and consent
psychosocial/privacy and reproductive counseling referral

unitMap.text: Retinal imaging and functional testing
coveredTopics: outer retinal bands/ellipsoid zone, ONL, schisis, deposits, atrophy
FAF patterns and light exposure; kinetic/static perimetry; fixation effects
avoid unsupported disease-specific claims from a single image

unitMap.text: Full-field ERG and electrophysiology
coveredTopics: ISCEV standard DA/LA protocol, waveforms, amplitude/implicit time
ERG is interpreted against laboratory reference methods and clinical phenotype
ERG may be unnecessary in select localized macular disease; follow current guidance

unitMap.text: Genetic testing, variants, and uncertain results
coveredTopics: panels/exome/genome, copy-number/deep intronic/structural blind spots
segregation/phase; pathogenicity frameworks; reanalysis
informed consent, genetic counseling, family cascade implications

unitMap.text: Rod-cone disease: RP spectrum and differential
coveredTopics: retinitis pigmentosa phenotypes; Usher and syndromic clues
vitamin A deficiency, autoimmune/paraneoplastic, drug toxicity and other mimics
cataract, cystoid macular edema, glaucoma and monitoring questions

unitMap.text: Cone-rod, macular dystrophies and phenocopies
coveredTopics: fundus flecks, vitelliform lesions, FAF/OCT and family history
cone dysfunction, photophobia, color/central acuity loss
age-related macular degeneration, toxic maculopathy and mimics

unitMap.text: Chorioretinal degeneration and syndromic IRD
coveredTopics: CHM-associated disease, gyrate atrophy; Usher and ciliopathy clues
audiology/ENT and genetics referral; systemic disease surveillance
phenotype-specific testing and limitations

unitMap.text: Pediatric assessment and family-centred care
coveredTopics: visual function in infants/young children; handheld OCT/ERG context
pediatric inherited retinal disease and differential
development, school/low-vision supports, assent/consent and caregiver counseling

unitMap.text: Therapy landscape and eligibility boundaries
coveredTopics: voretigene neparvovec: FDA indication is confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy; assess label/clinical criteria/current guidance
trial phases, gene replacement/editing/antisense concepts; ClinicalTrials.gov search literacy
risks, multidisciplinary evaluation, referral; never infer candidacy from diagnosis alone

unitMap.text: Longitudinal care, complications, low vision and access
coveredTopics: vision rehabilitation, assistive technology and driving/occupational counselling as appropriate
cataract/CME/other complications require individual ophthalmic evaluation
patient organisations/resources, shared decisions and follow-up

unitMap.text: Clinical trials, evidence, and capstone synthesis
coveredTopics: trial registry filters and status verification; endpoint/phase basics
fictional cases; multidisciplinary case conference; documentation and safety
integrate phenotype, multimodal testing, genetic report, counseling/management boundaries

topicGaps: The updated ledger contains 5.2333 conservatively verified specialty hours, leaving 30.7667 hours to the 36-hour video floor. Four additional unique free public recordings contribute only their observed transcript-time floors; exact player end runtimes were unavailable, and time beyond each last transcript timestamp is not credited.

Media topics still inadequately covered by verified recordings include dedicated pediatric examination/adaptation and sedation-risk reasoning; detailed multimodal imaging acquisition and interpretation; full variant-classification/assay-limit teaching; syndromic and chorioretinal degenerations; counseling and longitudinal rehabilitation; and current trial-by-trial eligibility. New recordings broaden phenotype, RP, complex-case, molecular-work-up and gene-therapy discussions but do not constitute a complete series.

Four complete original teaching episodes plus one introductory episode are scripted in the separate authored episode file. Scripts, the existing P-IRD clip briefs and the existing pilot remain unrendered and contribute zero video hours. The 36-hour floor is not reached by those plans or scripts.
The linked Cybersight ERG seminar is substantively relevant, but its exact duration could not be verified from the public page/accessible transcript in this check; it remains uncounted.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.
