topicGaps: The updated ledger contains 5.2333 conservatively verified specialty hours, leaving 30.7667 hours to the 36-hour video floor. Four additional unique free public recordings contribute only their observed transcript-time floors; exact player end runtimes were unavailable, and time beyond each last transcript timestamp is not credited.

Media topics still inadequately covered by verified recordings include dedicated pediatric examination/adaptation and sedation-risk reasoning; detailed multimodal imaging acquisition and interpretation; full variant-classification/assay-limit teaching; syndromic and chorioretinal degenerations; counseling and longitudinal rehabilitation; and current trial-by-trial eligibility. New recordings broaden phenotype, RP, complex-case, molecular-work-up and gene-therapy discussions but do not constitute a complete series.

Four complete original teaching episodes plus one introductory episode are scripted in the separate authored episode file. Scripts, the existing P-IRD clip briefs and the existing pilot remain unrendered and contribute zero video hours. The 36-hour floor is not reached by those plans or scripts.
The linked Cybersight ERG seminar is substantively relevant, but its exact duration could not be verified from the public page/accessible transcript in this check; it remains uncounted.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A young adult reports years of worsening night blindness in both eyes and gradually constricting peripheral fields. Which broad functional pattern is most consistent?

options.text: Primary rod dysfunction with generalized rod-cone disease
Acute optic neuritis
Isolated macular cone dysfunction
Retinal vascular occlusion

practiceQuestions.rationale: Nyctalopia and peripheral-field loss point toward rod-predominant dysfunction, but diagnosis requires examination and appropriate testing; this vignette is not diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected IRD has no known affected relatives. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Absence of family history excludes inherited disease
Family history can be negative due to recessive inheritance, small family, de novo variation, or incomplete information
Only mitochondrial disease remains possible
A genetic test is contraindicated

practiceQuestions.rationale: A negative pedigree does not rule out IRD; inheritance and family structure affect observed segregation.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a child with suspected IRD who cannot reliably perform visual fields, what principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Use identical adult test protocol regardless of age
Adapt functional/imaging tests to developmental capacity and weigh sedation risks against the information expected
Assume normal fields
Repeat non-recordable ERG indefinitely

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO guidance notes pediatric testing limitations and individualized consideration of sedation and reliable normative interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes a negative molecular panel in a clinically convincing IRD?

options.text: It proves the phenotype is acquired
It excludes all genetic causes
It does not necessarily exclude IRD because method and variant coverage have limitations
It proves the family history is inaccurate

practiceQuestions.rationale: Negative results can reflect assay limitations, unknown genes, or variants not detected; interpret with phenotype and genetics expertise.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which finding most directly supports obtaining broader systemic history and coordinated evaluation?

options.text: Retinal symptoms plus sensorineural hearing concerns
A single normal acuity measurement
A refractive error alone
A normal intraocular pressure

practiceQuestions.rationale: Syndromic IRD such as Usher syndrome warrants audiologic/ENT involvement and ongoing management as appropriate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has a localized macular dystrophy phenotype. Which test-selection statement is most accurate?

options.text: Full-field ERG is mandatory in every macular dystrophy
AAO guidance notes full-field ERG is not necessary in certain selected macular phenotypes, though differential diagnosis may justify it
ERG replaces imaging
An abnormal ERG alone identifies a causal gene

practiceQuestions.rationale: Testing should be selected by phenotype and differential; the AAO statement describes selected settings in which full-field ERG is unnecessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the FDA-labeled indication for voretigene neparvovec (LUXTURNA) in the US?

options.text: Any retinitis pigmentosa with severe vision loss
Confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy
Any pathogenic variant in any retinal gene
Any patient interested in gene therapy

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA lists the indication as confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy. Individual eligibility requires current label and specialist assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A single heterozygous pathogenic RPE65 variant is found. What conclusion is best?

options.text: This automatically meets the FDA indication
This alone does not establish the confirmed biallelic genotype required by the labeled indication
It means the patient has no retinal disease
Proceed directly to treatment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The FDA indication specifies confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutation-associated retinal dystrophy; do not infer eligibility from one allele.

practiceQuestions.stem: When comparing serial full-field ERGs, what is essential?

options.text: Ignore adaptation and recording conditions
Use standardized methods and appropriate reference data; note protocol deviations and clinical context
Compare raw amplitude across laboratories without qualification
Use only one flash response

practiceQuestions.rationale: ISCEV standardization supports consistency for diagnosis, monitoring and inter-laboratory comparisons.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the board credential/exam status relevant to this named IRD fellowship?

options.text: A distinct American Board of Inherited Retinal Degeneration examination
ABO certification is the general ophthalmology pathway; no separate IRD board exam is identified by the cited ABO source
Fellowship completion itself guarantees ABO certification
No board examination exists for ophthalmology

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO source describes general ophthalmology WQE and Oral Examination. The programme page does not confer board eligibility or establish a separate IRD board examination.

title: Glaucoma Fellowship

prerequisites.recommendedLearner: Physician learner with completed ophthalmology residency or equivalent background seeking advanced self-study; accessible as structured review for ophthalmology residents under faculty guidance.
priorKnowledge: Ocular anatomy/physiology, basic ophthalmic examination and imaging
Basic optics and interpretation of standard ophthalmic clinical records
prerequisites.notARequirementOrCredential: These are curricular recommendations, not programme eligibility; this course cannot confer physician status, fellowship entry eligibility, licensure, supervised experience, or board eligibility.

objectives: Synthesize glaucoma history, angle, IOP, optic-nerve structure and visual function evidence with calibrated uncertainty.
Interpret gonioscopy, perimetry, optic nerve/OCT and longitudinal data while identifying reliability limits and artifacts.
Compare primary and secondary glaucoma mechanisms and recognize urgent presentations for clinical escalation.
Discuss evidence-supported risk reduction, treatment classes and broad procedural goals without authorizing clinical intervention.
Evaluate glaucoma cases and literature with attention to rights, ethics, disparities, supervision and scope.

units.title: Glaucoma definitions, aqueous physiology, and a diagnostic frame
objectives: Explain aqueous production, conventional and uveoscleral outflow, and why IOP is a modifiable risk factor rather than a stand-alone diagnosis.
Construct a problem representation integrating symptoms, risk, examination, structure and function.
Distinguish measured pressure from disease and identify urgent red flags.
topics: Aqueous humor anatomy and dynamics; optic nerve injury; history and risk context; tonometry, pachymetry and measurement limits; baseline documentation.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—pathophysiology/basic science/risk assessment; presentation; diagnostic testing
units.casePractice: Use a fictional referral with one elevated IOP measurement and a normal-appearing nerve; identify missing tests before labeling disease.
units.assessment: One-page diagnostic frame: distinguish ocular hypertension, glaucoma suspect and established glaucoma; justify what evidence is still needed.

units.title: Gonioscopy, angle anatomy, and anterior-segment imaging
objectives: Describe angle landmarks and document angle findings reproducibly.
Compare indentation gonioscopy with anterior-segment OCT and ultrasound biomicroscopy, including limitations.
Recognize occludable angle and secondary angle mechanisms without treating imaging alone as a diagnosis.
topics: Dynamic gonioscopy; angle grading; peripheral anterior synechiae; plateau iris; lens-related crowding; AS-OCT/UBM correlation.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—primary angle-closure; secondary angle-closure; diagnostic testing
units.casePractice: Read linked, authentic Iowa angle cases; make an angle diagram from the text and state uncertainties.
units.assessment: Structured gonioscopy interpretation worksheet (angle, mechanism, extent, limitations), scored for reproducibility and differential.

units.title: Perimetry and functional loss
objectives: Assess reliability indices and common artifacts before interpreting automated fields.
Describe characteristic glaucomatous patterns and distinguish them from neurologic or other ocular causes.
Interpret change over time with appropriate test strategy and clinical context.
topics: Threshold perimetry; fixation losses/false responses; pattern deviation and hemifield test; central testing; learning effects; progression.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—presentation and diagnostic testing; visual loss differential
units.casePractice: Interpret only publicly linked educational fields at EyeRounds; do not download/rehost images.
units.assessment: Timed five-field station: reliability, pattern, localization, next test and one confounder for each.

units.title: Optic nerve, OCT, and longitudinal structure-function synthesis
objectives: Describe optic nerve/RNFL/macular ganglion-cell findings and their limitations.
Detect artifacts and avoid overcalling normative database classifications.
Integrate structural and functional tests to assess progression.
topics: Disc anatomy, rim/notching, hemorrhage, RNFL and ganglion-cell analysis; segmentation/myopia artifacts; structure-function discordance; serial comparison.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—diagnostic testing; presentation; progression/outcomes
units.casePractice: Analyze a linked case with discordant OCT and field, state two artifact alternatives and propose a confirmatory plan.
units.assessment: Short-answer imaging interpretation, graded on data quality, artifact recognition, and justified inference.

units.title: Ocular hypertension and glaucoma suspects
objectives: Apply established risk factors and longitudinal evidence to a suspect assessment.
Explain the OHTS-derived rationale for selective treatment and the individualized nature of target IOP.
Document a surveillance plan proportionate to risk without converting population evidence into certainty for an individual.
topics: OHTS; suspect definitions; risk factors; conversion evidence; monitoring; shared decision-making.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—glaucoma suspect; risk assessment; testing; management/outcomes
units.casePractice: Fictional suspect cases with differing risk profiles; compare treat-now versus observe-and-retest reasoning.
units.assessment: Risk memo: identify evidence, uncertainty, a monitoring plan and a treatment threshold; rubric rewards calibrated language.

units.title: POAG, normal-tension glaucoma, and progression management
objectives: Synthesize open angle, optic-nerve, OCT and field findings into a supported diagnosis.
Set and revise an individualized target using baseline, severity, rate of change, life context and treatment burden.
Recognize when normal-range IOP does not exclude glaucoma and consider competing optic neuropathies.
topics: POAG/juvenile-onset; normal-tension phenotype; disc hemorrhage; longitudinal progression; treatment response and reassessment.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—primary open-angle; glaucoma suspect; management/outcomes; differential
units.casePractice: Fictional normal-IOP progressive field loss scenario; assess alternative optic neuropathy and treatment evidence without asserting a single sign is pathognomonic.
units.assessment: Two longitudinal case analyses with defended target, monitoring endpoint and a revision trigger.

units.title: Primary angle closure and acute angle-closure presentations
objectives: Differentiate anatomic narrow angles, angle closure and angle-closure glaucoma.
Recognize an acute painful red-eye/nausea presentation as an emergency requiring immediate assessment.
Compare laser and lens/surgical pathways in context of anatomy, disease and current guidance.
topics: Pupillary block, plateau iris, synechial closure, acute versus chronic disease, fellow-eye assessment, treatment principles and limitations.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—primary angle-closure; presentation; testing; management/complications
units.casePractice: Use linked plateau-iris and aqueous-misdirection case resources; identify mechanism clues and escalation needs.
units.assessment: Emergency-vignette oral reasoning station, explicitly educational; score recognition, differential, immediate referral/escalation and limits.

units.title: Secondary open-angle glaucoma
objectives: Organize secondary open-angle causes by mechanism and history/exam clues.
Recognize steroid response, pigment dispersion, exfoliation, inflammatory and traumatic mechanisms.
Identify cause-directed evaluation and monitoring without inferring causality from one clue.
topics: Pseudoexfoliation; pigmentary; steroid response; uveitic; traumatic/angle recession; elevated episcleral venous pressure; neovascular and tumor-associated disease.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—secondary glaucomas, open angle; history/exam; testing; pathophysiology
units.casePractice: Compare fictional and linked cases; separate cause, association, and consequence; review image terms before any class use.
units.assessment: Mechanism matrix with differential, supporting/contradicting evidence, and next diagnostic step; no image reproduction.

units.title: Secondary angle closure, lens, postsurgical and complex glaucoma
objectives: Distinguish pupillary block from non-pupillary-block mechanisms.
Recognize lens-, inflammation-, trauma-, postsurgical-, and aqueous-misdirection mechanisms.
Explain why mechanism-specific urgent assessment matters and identify uncertainty.
topics: Lens-associated; aqueous misdirection; nanophthalmos; post-cataract/aphakic and corneal transplant-associated; epithelial downgrowth; iris/ciliary tumors/cysts; hypotony context.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—secondary angle-closure; post-surgical glaucomas; diagnostic reasoning
units.casePractice: Linked EyeRounds aqueous misdirection, nanophthalmos and lens-associated cases; learners state which missing data prevent a firm conclusion.
units.assessment: Oral mechanism map with safety red flags and a concise differential.

units.title: Medical and laser therapy: mechanism, evidence, safety
objectives: Compare classes by mechanism and common contraindication/interactions using current references.
Explain initial and revised IOP targets as goals rather than universal rules.
Compare trabeculoplasty, iridotomy and iridoplasty indications conceptually; no unsupervised procedural instruction.
topics: Prostaglandin analogues; beta blockers; alpha agonists; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; trabecular outflow agents; hyperosmotic agents; laser treatment; adherence and access.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—management/outcomes/complications; basic science
units.casePractice: Fictional medication reconciliation exercise; identify systemic context and avoid proposing patient-specific medication changes.
units.assessment: Evidence comparison and safety table, scored for mechanism, major caveats, evidence citation and patient-centered monitoring.

units.title: Incisional glaucoma surgery and postoperative complications
objectives: Compare broad goals and tradeoffs of trabeculectomy, drainage devices, MIGS and cyclodestructive procedures.
Recognize postoperative complication categories and the need for supervised clinical assessment.
Interpret outcomes and evidence without treating a video as procedural competence.
topics: Trabeculectomy; tube shunts; minimally invasive glaucoma surgery; combined cataract/glaucoma procedures; cyclodestruction; hypotony, bleb leak, infection, choroidal effusion; quality/outcomes.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—post-surgical; management/outcomes/complications/prognosis
units.casePractice: Observe only linked educational surgical/case materials; discuss postoperative complication recognition, no copied video or operative checklist.
units.assessment: Comparative procedure rationale and complication-response essay; no procedural skill is assessed or certified.

units.title: Pediatric, congenital, genetic and research/scholarship themes
objectives: Recognize pediatric glaucoma presentation patterns and the role of specialist evaluation.
Differentiate congenital/developmental syndromic associations from confirmed etiology in a case.
Critically appraise glaucoma literature, outcomes and evidence gaps with ethical handling of images/data.
topics: Primary congenital and juvenile-onset glaucoma; anterior-segment dysgenesis; phacomatoses; pediatric surgical principles; research design, communication, ethics, disparities and scholarship.
boardDomains: Glaucoma—secondary/open and angle closure; presentation/testing/management; pathology/landmark studies/ethics as cross-cutting ABO context
units.casePractice: Use linked de-identified/consented educational pediatric case pages only under the host license; no downloaded images or records.
units.assessment: Journal-club critique with PICO, bias, applicability, ethics and a one-page literature-supported teaching note.

assignment.title: Glaucoma evidence-and-reasoning portfolio (fictional cases only)
deliverables: (1) one structured suspect workup and risk memo; (2) two paired structure/function interpretations with reliability/artifact commentary; (3) one mechanism-based secondary-glaucoma differential; (4) one evidence critique of a glaucoma guideline/study; (5) a brief oral-board-style case summary that identifies uncertainty and escalation limits.

rubric.standard: Integrates available evidence and plausible alternatives; does not overstate certainty.
Checks gonioscopy, perimetry reliability, OCT artifacts and longitudinal evidence.
Cites current AAO/NEI/AUPO/ABO sources and distinguishes policy from clinical recommendations.
Identifies urgent signals, escalation, shared decisions and limits; never offers unsupervised treatment/procedure advice.
Concise, interpretable, properly cited work; links to case sources and reuses no unlicensed images.

assignment.passStandard: Suggested course threshold 80/100 for self-study progression only; not validated, not a board predictor, and not clinical competence.

formative: Retrieval checks after each unit; case-based field/OCT reasoning; answer rationales; study log.
summative: Ten original multiple-choice items in this course packet; portfolio scored against the transparent rubric; learner self-explanation and error log.
assessment.limitations: No psychometric validation, clinical review or board endorsement. Scores cannot predict examination passage, certify competence, authorize procedures or establish licensure.

studyHours.plan: A transparent independent study plan: 36 recorded-video hours (target floor) plus approximately 48 hours of readings, case reasoning, written assignments, spaced review, and feedback; expected total 84 hours. The 36-hour target is not met by current external videos. Study-plan time is not verified video time.

unitMap.text: Glaucoma definitions, aqueous physiology, and a diagnostic frame
coveredTopics: Aqueous humor anatomy and dynamics; optic nerve injury; history and risk context; tonometry, pachymetry and measurement limits; baseline documentation.

unitMap.text: Gonioscopy, angle anatomy, and anterior-segment imaging
coveredTopics: Dynamic gonioscopy; angle grading; peripheral anterior synechiae; plateau iris; lens-related crowding; AS-OCT/UBM correlation.

unitMap.text: Perimetry and functional loss
coveredTopics: Threshold perimetry; fixation losses/false responses; pattern deviation and hemifield test; central testing; learning effects; progression.

unitMap.text: Optic nerve, OCT, and longitudinal structure-function synthesis
coveredTopics: Disc anatomy, rim/notching, hemorrhage, RNFL and ganglion-cell analysis; segmentation/myopia artifacts; structure-function discordance; serial comparison.

unitMap.text: Ocular hypertension and glaucoma suspects
coveredTopics: OHTS; suspect definitions; risk factors; conversion evidence; monitoring; shared decision-making.

unitMap.text: POAG, normal-tension glaucoma, and progression management
coveredTopics: POAG/juvenile-onset; normal-tension phenotype; disc hemorrhage; longitudinal progression; treatment response and reassessment.

unitMap.text: Primary angle closure and acute angle-closure presentations
coveredTopics: Pupillary block, plateau iris, synechial closure, acute versus chronic disease, fellow-eye assessment, treatment principles and limitations.

unitMap.text: Secondary open-angle glaucoma
coveredTopics: Pseudoexfoliation; pigmentary; steroid response; uveitic; traumatic/angle recession; elevated episcleral venous pressure; neovascular and tumor-associated disease.

unitMap.text: Secondary angle closure, lens, postsurgical and complex glaucoma
coveredTopics: Lens-associated; aqueous misdirection; nanophthalmos; post-cataract/aphakic and corneal transplant-associated; epithelial downgrowth; iris/ciliary tumors/cysts; hypotony context.

unitMap.text: Medical and laser therapy: mechanism, evidence, safety
coveredTopics: Prostaglandin analogues; beta blockers; alpha agonists; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; trabecular outflow agents; hyperosmotic agents; laser treatment; adherence and access.

unitMap.text: Incisional glaucoma surgery and postoperative complications
coveredTopics: Trabeculectomy; tube shunts; minimally invasive glaucoma surgery; combined cataract/glaucoma procedures; cyclodestruction; hypotony, bleb leak, infection, choroidal effusion; quality/outcomes.

unitMap.text: Pediatric, congenital, genetic and research/scholarship themes
coveredTopics: Primary congenital and juvenile-onset glaucoma; anterior-segment dysgenesis; phacomatoses; pediatric surgical principles; research design, communication, ethics, disparities and scholarship.

topicGaps: No additional recording met the combined unique-media, free-access, and observed-runtime evidence test; the external ledger remains the existing 50 short Iowa lectures (11.6983 h).
Fellowship-level supervised examination, independent case responsibility, surgical/laser performance, complication response, and feedback remain wholly unavailable from self-study recordings.

Advanced perimetry/OCT interpretation and longitudinal progression assessment require more depth than the short introductory sequence; discordant results, artifacts, device limits, and alternate optic neuropathies need further sourced teaching.

Complex secondary and angle-closure mechanisms, contemporary evidence comparison, individualized management trade-offs, postoperative outcomes/complications, and pediatric/genetic glaucoma remain insufficiently covered at fellowship depth.

Investigated Moran CORE and Glaucoma Foundation full-session recordings are documented separately, but their player access and/or exact runtimes were not verified without bypassing public anti-bot restrictions; no candidate duration is counted.

Current AAO guidance, board outlines, AUPO requirements, eligibility rules, and clinical recommendations require ongoing qualified human review; no human clinician review was performed for this expansion.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional vignette: an asymptomatic adult has one IOP reading of 25 mmHg in one eye, normal-appearing discs by the referring note, and no visual-field or gonioscopy data. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Diagnose POAG and prescribe two agents
Obtain a complete glaucoma evaluation including repeat/validated IOP, gonioscopy, nerve/OCT and perimetry, then stratify risk
Rule out glaucoma because no symptoms are present
Proceed directly to incisional surgery

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single pressure value is not itself established optic neuropathy; the suspect workup uses gonioscopy, pachymetry, tonometry, perimetry, nerve exam and OCT, then risk-based decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A treated glaucoma suspect has persistently elevated IOP but no evidence of conversion. Which statement best matches the AAO suspect PPP?

options.text: Every suspect must be treated to 30% below baseline
Treatment depends on IOP and associated risk factors; a reasonable initial target when treatment is chosen is 20% reduction
Treatment is never appropriate without a field defect
A single IOP threshold dictates treatment for every patient

practiceQuestions.rationale: The suspect PPP describes selective risk-based treatment; if treatment is chosen a 20% target is a reasonable starting point based on OHTS, not a universal mandate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional longitudinal data show repeatable arcuate field loss, matching focal RNFL thinning and open angles. Which synthesis is most defensible?

options.text: Concordant structure and function with an open angle supports POAG when secondary causes are excluded
A normal IOP on one visit excludes glaucoma
OCT alone establishes the exact disease mechanism
A field defect is diagnostic regardless of reliability

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAO describes characteristic POAG features as open gonioscopy, glaucomatous nerve change, RNFL/macular thinning and typical field loss with secondary causes excluded.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational acute vignette includes sudden severe eye pain, red eye, blurred vision, nausea and a shallow peripheral chamber. What is the safest general interpretation?

options.text: Routine review in six months
Possible acute angle closure requiring immediate eye/emergency assessment
A benign side effect of reading
A diagnosis of chronic open-angle glaucoma

practiceQuestions.rationale: NEI describes this symptom cluster as an angle-closure emergency; this educational question does not authorize treatment or delay emergency assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A normal-range IOP is recorded in a fictional patient with progressive glaucomatous field change. Which claim is accurate?

options.text: Normal-range pressure rules out glaucoma
Normal-tension glaucoma exists and IOP lowering may still be beneficial
Only elevated IOP damages the optic nerve
A single normal reading establishes stability

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO POAG PPP recognizes patients with untreated IOP in normal range; lowering IOP benefits many. Interpretation still requires assessment for alternative optic neuropathies and progression.

practiceQuestions.stem: An eye with a history of blunt trauma later shows elevated IOP and angle recession on gonioscopy. Which category best fits?

options.text: Secondary open-angle glaucoma due to trauma
Primary pupillary-block angle closure
Primary congenital glaucoma
Pseudoexfoliation by definition

practiceQuestions.rationale: Angle recession after trauma is a secondary open-angle mechanism; corroborate with history and exam rather than assuming causality from pressure alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with uveitis receives topical corticosteroid and develops raised IOP. Which statement best captures the differential?

options.text: Steroid response and inflammatory outflow damage are possible, and both clinical context and cause-directed evaluation matter
The pressure elevation proves primary POAG
Steroid exposure excludes uveitic glaucoma
No monitoring is needed once inflammation improves

practiceQuestions.rationale: NEI and the glaucoma curriculum describe both uveitis-related mechanisms and steroid-induced pressure elevation; the vignette cannot distinguish them without clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees an abnormal OCT classification with a normal repeat visual field in a highly myopic eye. What is the best action?

options.text: Treat the OCT color code as definitive progression
Review scan quality, segmentation and anatomy; correlate with repeat fields and prior structural/clinical data
Ignore all OCT data forever
Diagnose neurologic disease immediately

practiceQuestions.rationale: Structural and functional tests are complementary; artifacts and anatomy can mislead isolated OCT interpretation. Correlation and longitudinal change are essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional fellow compares a surgical clip to an operative competency assessment. Which is correct?

options.text: Watching video certifies independent surgical competence
Surgical competence requires supervised training and assessment; a public clip is educational only
Video substitutes for a clinical fellowship
No supervision is required after online viewing

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUPO requirements specify supervised clinical and operative fellowship training and evaluation. Videos do not create procedural competence or clinical authorization.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which board statement is supported by the official ABO sources reviewed?

options.text: A separate ABO glaucoma subspecialty board exam is established
ABO describes general ophthalmology written and oral certification exams; glaucoma is a WQE content domain, and no separate glaucoma board exam was identified in reviewed sources
Completing a fellowship automatically grants ABO certification
A self-study course creates board eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO sources define comprehensive ophthalmology certification through WQE and oral examinations after qualifying training; its WQE outline includes glaucoma at 14%. No separate fellowship board exam is listed in reviewed official materials.

coveredTopics: Preconception and antenatal prevention; anemia/infection screening; hypertensive risk; gestational age; referral pathways; continuity.

coveredTopics: Labour progress; fetal/maternal surveillance; emergency readiness; referral; companionship; documentation; WHO intrapartum recommendations.

unitMap.text: Gynecologic health, cervical cancer prevention, and essential surgery

unitMap.text: Clinical research ethics, epidemiology, and implementation science
coveredTopics: PICO/PEO; bias; sample frames; missingness; mixed methods; implementation frameworks; authorship; data governance; local leadership.

topicGaps: Obstetric and gynecologic clinical systems across antenatal, labour, postpartum and gynecologic care remain only partially represented by short public recordings; no supervised clinical cases or procedural competency are represented.
Maternal measurement/ascertainment: the packet’s compendium link is blocked by NCBI verification; use WHO ICD-MM and indicator metadata, with local data-quality limits explicit.

Hypertensive disorders, hemorrhage, obstructed labour, thromboembolism, sepsis and surgical emergencies: recordings are overviews, not protocol-complete training; current local algorithms, escalation and competent supervision remain required.
Antenatal screening, risk assessment and continuity require current national protocols; no comprehensive verified public lecture sequence located.
Postnatal maternal-newborn continuity, mental health and referral are only partly addressed by the recorded lactation episode and 2022 WHO guideline reading.

Voluntary contraception is represented by U.S.-specific MEC and rights-oriented lectures; international method eligibility, provision rules, abortion law and service pathways remain jurisdiction-specific and incompletely taught.

Gynecologic cancer prevention is the strongest new recording expansion (FIND cervical series), but it is South Africa-contextual and does not replace current WHO/national algorithms, pathology capacity, treatment referral, or hands-on colposcopy/surgery.

Research design, human-subject review, mixed methods, data governance, causal inference and implementation-science competencies have readings and limited contextual lectures, but no complete free lecture series was verified.

Maternal death review and quality improvement have CDC resources and the existing Stanford recording; local review governance, confidentiality, audit-to-action and evaluation need original instruction.
Reciprocal partnership, predeparture preparation, supervision, sustainability, handover and policy translation remain largely original-teaching/mentored-learning needs.

boardNames: American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) — primary certification in Obstetrics and Gynecology; separate subspecialty boards are Complex Family Planning, Gynecologic Oncology, Maternal-Fetal Medicine, Reproductive Endocrinology & Infertility, and Urogynecology & Reproductive Pelvic Surgery. No separate Global Women’s Health board exam/certificate was identified in ABOG’s published list.
medical.boardStatus: Institutional clinical physician fellowship, not a distinct ABOG subspecialty board. ABOG board subspecialty page was dynamic and its text could not be fetched; public ABOG search results enumerate five subspecialties and exclude global women’s health. This is an evidence-limited negative finding, date checked 2026-10-07; recheck ABOG directly before relying on it.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: BWH states applicants must complete a four-year ACGME-approved OB/GYN residency and be eligible for Massachusetts medical licensure; fellowship participation/degree does not itself confer ABOG eligibility, certification, licensure, or an independent specialty credential. Verify individual credential status with ABOG and current program.

officialProgrammes.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital (Mass General Brigham; Harvard Medical School affiliate)
officialProgrammes.name: BWH Global Women’s Health/Obstetrics and Gynecology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a 24-month clinical physician fellowship: four months BWH clinical work in year one; 12 months at an approved international partner site during years one/two; four months BWH clinical work; MPH in two intensive summers; project/publication/presentation expectation. Page states 4-year ACGME-accredited OB/GYN residency and Massachusetts licensure eligibility as applicant requirements. It is programme-specific, not ACGME/ABOG accreditation proof for this fellowship.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This item is one named BWH institutional clinical physician fellowship, not generic directory category, not a combined residency programme, and not a research-only/non-physician supplement. ACOG’s resources (last current as of Oct 2020) list a distinct Johns Hopkins Global Women’s Health Fellowship; that is a separately named programme and is not merged as a BWH variant. A 2024 literature review finds US programmes vary; details must be checked individually. The current Johns Hopkins Medicine page confirms a distinct two-year interprofessional Global Women’s Health Fellowship pairing physicians with other health professionals, with clinical/education/research and systems-strengthening aims. It has different eligibility: US physician applicants are OB/GYN residency-complete and ABOG eligible/certified; LMIC physicians from several specialties are eligible; nursing/midwifery applicants have separate requirements. Its page carries a stale dated 2024 application note, so current cohort availability is not confirmed. It remains a separate institutional offering, not merged with BWH; the packet’s BWH-specific physician curriculum is the course scope.
sourceCaveats: The BWH programme page was fetched and directly describes the particular fellowship; public page content can change.

ABOG subspecialty page was dynamically rendered with content unavailable on fetch. Search results from ABOG enumerate five subspecialties; absence of GWH is a bounded finding, not a guarantee of future board policy.
ACOG fellowship directory explicitly says resources are current as of October 2020. Hopkins is a distinct named program in that archive, not merged into BWH offering; current status was not verified.
NCBI pages for WHO compendium and 2024 fellowship review triggered browser-verification challenges. Search metadata was used only for discovery; no detailed facts from these pages are asserted.

Recorded videos are public and their visible runtimes were observed on YouTube pages; availability/access may change. V001 is US-focused maternal health equity lecture; V002 is general global health foundation. Video V003 has unknown duration and is not counted.
Clinical source updates may supersede readings. Local law, guidelines, services and scope vary. Human clinical review has not been performed.

unknownDurationItems.reason: Accessible duration not structurally supported by evidence.

topicGaps: Obstetric and gynecologic clinical systems across antenatal, labour, postpartum and gynecologic care remain only partially represented by short public recordings; no supervised clinical cases or procedural competency are represented.
Maternal measurement/ascertainment: the packet’s compendium link is blocked by NCBI verification; use WHO ICD-MM and indicator metadata, with local data-quality limits explicit.

Hypertensive disorders, hemorrhage, obstructed labour, thromboembolism, sepsis and surgical emergencies: recordings are overviews, not protocol-complete training; current local algorithms, escalation and competent supervision remain required.
Antenatal screening, risk assessment and continuity require current national protocols; no comprehensive verified public lecture sequence located.
Postnatal maternal-newborn continuity, mental health and referral are only partly addressed by the recorded lactation episode and 2022 WHO guideline reading.

Voluntary contraception is represented by U.S.-specific MEC and rights-oriented lectures; international method eligibility, provision rules, abortion law and service pathways remain jurisdiction-specific and incompletely taught.

Gynecologic cancer prevention is the strongest new recording expansion (FIND cervical series), but it is South Africa-contextual and does not replace current WHO/national algorithms, pathology capacity, treatment referral, or hands-on colposcopy/surgery.

Research design, human-subject review, mixed methods, data governance, causal inference and implementation-science competencies have readings and limited contextual lectures, but no complete free lecture series was verified.

Maternal death review and quality improvement have CDC resources and the existing Stanford recording; local review governance, confidentiality, audit-to-action and evaluation need original instruction.
Reciprocal partnership, predeparture preparation, supervision, sustainability, handover and policy translation remain largely original-teaching/mentored-learning needs.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes this fellowship from a board subspecialty?

options.text: Global women’s health is one of ABOG’s five subspecialty certificates.
BWH describes a 24-month physician fellowship; ABOG’s published subspecialty list does not include global women’s health.
Completion automatically grants ABOG certification.
Every global-health fellow must take an ABOG subspecialty exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BWH page describes an institutional 24-month fellowship. ABOG lists five subspecialty certificates; global women’s health is not among those listed. This is not evidence that graduates qualify for any other credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: An international elective is proposed. What is the safest educational framing?

options.text: Allow learners to practice beyond their home scope to compensate for local shortages.
Set competency goals, supervision, support, ethical safeguards, and local resource limits before departure.
Count the elective as a substitute for required chief-resident experience.
Use the visit mainly to collect publishable cases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME guidance calls for defined goals, supervision, adequate support/resources, ethical practice, predeparture preparation, and work within training scope; it notes global experience cannot count toward required chief experience.

practiceQuestions.stem: A project reports maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. What is this measure?

options.text: Maternal mortality ratio
Maternal case-fatality ratio
Perinatal mortality rate
Maternal death rate per woman-year

practiceQuestions.rationale: The maternal mortality ratio uses maternal deaths divided by live births, typically expressed per 100,000 live births; interpret ascertainment and timing definitions in the source.

practiceQuestions.stem: A contraceptive condition-method pairing is U.S. MEC category 3. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: No restriction.
Advantages generally outweigh risks.
Risks usually outweigh advantages; use is usually not recommended unless more appropriate options are unavailable or unacceptable, with clinical judgment.
Unacceptable health risk in every circumstance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC defines category 3 as risks usually outweighing advantages and generally not recommended unless alternatives are unavailable or unacceptable; category 4 is unacceptable risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: A district proposes a maternity intervention copied from a high-resource hospital. What is the strongest first step?

options.text: Replicate the protocol unchanged.
Co-design with local clinicians and communities; map staffing, referral, equipment, legal, and continuity constraints.
Choose the intervention based on donor availability alone.
Begin data collection before ethics and governance review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Global practice requires local partnership and context-sensitive feasibility, ethical review, and sustainability. These are curriculum principles, not a claim about any partner site.

practiceQuestions.stem: A maternal death review identifies delayed referral, unavailable blood, and poor handoff. Which response fits a learning system?

options.text: Attribute the outcome solely to the last clinician.
Conduct confidential, non-punitive systems review and assign measurable actions across the referral pathway.
Publish identifiable details to promote accountability.
Use mortality counts alone as proof the intervention worked.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Review should protect confidentiality and examine system contributors; actions and process/outcome measures must be explicit and proportionate.

practiceQuestions.stem: WHO intrapartum care recommendations are used in a low-resource site. What is an appropriate interpretation?

options.text: They are a universal substitute for national protocols and clinical judgment.
They inform local policy/protocol development and should be adapted to capacity and context.
They authorize any intervention if the guideline mentions it.
They are only for high-income hospitals.

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO says the guideline informs national and local policies/protocols and is designed to address varied service settings; it is not a direct authorization for unsupervised care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A proposed program reports improved attendance but no maternal outcome changes. Which inference is justified?

options.text: The intervention reduced maternal mortality.
The program may have changed a service-use process measure; causal/outcome effects remain unestablished.
Attendance proves equity improved.
No further evaluation is needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Attendance is a process/uptake measure and does not establish clinical causal benefit or equity impact without suitable design, denominator, and outcome measures.

practiceQuestions.stem: When using a public clinical image repository in teaching, what is the proper default?

options.text: Free access permits downloading and redistribution.
Link to source and follow license/permission; do not reproduce or upload unless expressly allowed.
Remove the watermark and cite it.
Use any image if de-identified.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view is not a reuse license. Follow repository rights and privacy terms; this curriculum does not copy patient images.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pregnancy/childbirth case is assembled by the course team and not derived from a patient. How should it be labelled?

options.text: Authentic case record
Fictional educational scenario
De-identified chart
Board question

title: Complex Benign Gynecology Fellowship
prerequisites: For course discussion: prior medical/OB-GYN training recommended; advanced reading assumes familiarity with pelvic anatomy, reproductive endocrinology, imaging and core obstetrics/gynecology.
For the real AAGL CBGF: completion of an obstetrics and gynecology residency is a requirement in AAGL program requirements; this independent course cannot satisfy it.
No prior operative experience is assumed or granted. All procedural learning in practice requires accredited supervised training and institutional authorization.
objectives: Synthesize current open and date-stamped guidelines across endometriosis, fibroids, abnormal uterine bleeding and chronic pelvic pain.
Interpret imaging questions and limitations and identify appropriate specialist referral pathways.
Compare benign gynecologic treatment options based on symptoms, anatomy, preferences, future fertility goals and evidence uncertainty.
Analyze preoperative risks, complications, consent and multidisciplinary roles without teaching unsupervised operative maneuvers.
Critically appraise clinical studies, case reports and program/certification claims.
Explain the distinction between AAGL CBGF program accreditation, ABOG primary certification, voluntary MIGS FPD and independent self-study.

boardNames: American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG)—Obstetrics and Gynecology primary specialty certification
ABOG Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (MIGS) Focused Practice Designation (voluntary FPD with a separate examination pathway; not a CBG subspecialty board certificate)
medical.boardStatus: No separate ABMS/ABOG subspecialty board certificate titled Complex Benign Gynecology (CBG) was identified in the current ABMS certificate list. ABOG states it offers voluntary MIGS and Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology Focused Practice Designations. The ABOG MIGS FPD examination is distinct from an independent CBG board certification; current application/exam eligibility, case-log rules and fees must be checked in ABOG’s live bulletin. AAGL accredits CBGF programs; the BWH program sheet listed accreditation period 2022–2026 and the AAGL 2026 CBG listing includes Brigham. Renewal beyond the listed period was not verified.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This educational course provides no medical degree, ACGME/AAGL fellowship credit, board eligibility, board preparation guarantee, license, privileges, procedural competence or certification. Real CBGF entry requires completion of obstetrics/gynecology residency per AAGL program requirements; ABOG primary board and FPD eligibility are controlled solely by ABOG’s current rules.

officialProgrammes.name: BWH Benign Gynecology Fellowship (current institutional page uses Complex Benign Gynecology—CBG; historic AAGL program sheet calls it MIGS)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page describes a two-year clinical physician fellowship focused on complex endometriosis/fibroids; laparoscopy, robotics, hysteroscopy, urogynecology, pain clinic and ultrasound; Faulkner rotation and a month-long Newton-Wellesley fellowship swap; research and teaching. AAGL directory lists Brigham for 2026; 2026 NRMP listing says not participating. AAGL program PDF dated 2025 reports accreditation period 2022–2026. As of 7 Oct 2026, post-2026 renewal status is not verified.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This packet records one exact institutional variant (BWH), which is listed in the saved supplemental discovery packet, the MGB institutional page and AAGL 2026 program directory. Faulkner Hospital and Newton-Wellesley are rotation/swap sites described by BWH, not separate program variants in this item. This is a clinical physician fellowship, not a research-only or non-physician course and not a combined residency. The official AAGL source documents AAGL CBGF accreditation; current post-2026 BWH reaccreditation and ACGME status were not confirmed. AAGL program accreditation must not be misrepresented as ACGME accreditation.
sourceCaveats: The ACOG 2026 diagnosis guideline full content is member/journal subscriber gated. No authentication workaround was used; public announcement and NICE/ESHRE sources are used within their actual scope.

The current AAGL 2026 directory lists BWH, while BWH’s 2025 program sheet states accreditation period 2022–2026. Renewal after that period was not independently verified; reconfirm with AAGL/BWH for future cohorts.

ABOG FPD rules change; the current exam bulletin should be consulted for specific candidate eligibility, case-log and examination requirements. This is a voluntary focused-practice designation, not a separate CBG board certificate.
No separate ACGME accreditation statement for BWH was located in this public-source review; AAGL accreditation and ACGME accreditation are not interchangeable.
YouTube metadata requests returned HTTP 403 / bot challenge. This was not bypassed. No runtimes or free-access statuses were inferred.
Public BWH/AAGL program descriptions are not complete proprietary institutional syllabi or live operative curricula. Rotation descriptions do not guarantee individual exposure or competence.
Clinical guidance and drug/device indications are jurisdiction- and date-sensitive. Check current primary sources and local protocols. Clinical content has not had human clinical review.
Case reports are authentic published narratives, but anonymization/consent and reuse rights were not independently inspected in all source pages; no patient records or images are reproduced.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has cyclic pelvic pain and a normal pelvic examination and routine transvaginal ultrasound. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Normal initial imaging excludes endometriosis.
A normal exam or scan does not exclude endometriosis; persistent symptoms may still warrant referral/evaluation.
CA-125 should be used to confirm the diagnosis.
Diagnostic laparoscopy is mandatory before any treatment discussion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE advises not to exclude endometriosis after normal exam or ultrasound and supports referral when symptoms persist or are impactful. NICE also says not to use CA-125 diagnostically. The exact updated ACOG full guideline is member/subscriber-gated.

practiceQuestions.stem: For suspected bowel/ureter deep endometriosis, what is an appropriate next diagnostic step before considering operative planning?

options.text: Rely only on CA-125.
Specialist transvaginal ultrasound or pelvic MRI interpreted by a specialist in gynecologic imaging.
Repeat a blind endometrial biopsy.
No imaging is useful.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE recommends specialist transvaginal ultrasound or pelvic MRI to diagnose deep disease and assess extent, planned/interpreted by an expert; specialist imaging before operative laparoscopy is appropriate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which lab test does the NICE HMB guideline recommend for all patients with heavy menstrual bleeding, in parallel with treatment?

options.text: Full blood count
Routine female hormone panel
Thyroid panel in every patient

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE NG88 recommends full blood count for all patients with HMB; hormone tests and thyroid testing are not routine without additional indication.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with persistent intermenstrual bleeding and risk factors for endometrial pathology needs evaluation. Which NICE pathway is supported?

options.text: Blind biopsy as the sole procedure
Outpatient hysteroscopy, with endometrial sampling at hysteroscopy when indicated
MRI as universal first-line
D&C as treatment

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE NG88 recommends outpatient hysteroscopy where history suggests submucosal fibroid, polyp or endometrial pathology; if sampling is needed, sample in the context of diagnostic hysteroscopy rather than blind biopsy.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which principle best reflects NICE guidance for HMB when treatment is being chosen?

options.text: Choose based only on measured blood loss.
Consider preferences, comorbidities, fibroid size/location/number and associated symptoms.
Recommend hysterectomy to every patient with fibroids.
Do not discuss fertility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE prioritizes quality-of-life impact and individualized choice, including uterine/fertility preferences, comorbidities, anatomy and symptoms.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient prioritizes future fertility and has symptomatic fibroids. What should counseling do?

options.text: State that UAE and myomectomy have identical pregnancy evidence.
Discuss options and uncertainty about reproductive consequences; myomectomy may preserve the uterus but is not a guarantee of fertility.
Recommend hysterectomy.
Promise no recurrence after myomectomy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE and ACOG patient information support individualized discussion of fertility effects; ACOG notes myomectomy preserves the uterus but scarring and future procedures are possible. Avoid promises.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has deep endometriosis involving suspected bowel or ureter. What service configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Single specialty surgical planning without imaging.
Specialist multidisciplinary service with advanced gynecologic expertise and access to colorectal/urology, imaging, pain and fertility expertise as relevant.
Treat the lesion stage alone.
No follow-up is indicated.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE lists multidisciplinary access for specialist endometriosis services, including colorectal, urology, pain, specialist imaging and fertility services.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which conclusion can be drawn from a single rare case report of diaphragmatic endometriosis?

options.text: It establishes comparative effectiveness of a treatment.
It describes an authentic reported clinical presentation but cannot establish population-level effectiveness or dictate a treatment choice.
It guarantees the same response in other patients.
It replaces guideline review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Case reports can illustrate uncommon presentations but are not comparative trials or practice guidelines; the linked source is used for appraisal only.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately distinguishes CBGF program accreditation from board status?

options.text: AAGL-accredited CBGF completion itself is an ABOG subspecialty board certificate.
AAGL accredits CBGF programs; ABOG lists a voluntary MIGS Focused Practice Designation, which is distinct from a CBG subspecialty board certificate.
CBGF is a non-physician certificate only.
There is no ABOG MIGS FPD examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAGL describes the CBGF Board as accrediting CBGF programs. ABOG states it offers voluntary MIGS FPD; ABMS certificate list does not list Complex Benign Gynecology as an ABOG subspecialty certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which training activity is necessary to establish operative competence in a real fellowship?

options.text: Watching online clips only.
Supervised clinical experience, simulation as applicable, documented assessment and required case logs.
Passing this independent course only.
Reading a case report.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAGL requirements specify supervised clinical activities, simulation/didactics and surgical competency/case log tracking; this self-study course does not confer procedural competence.
